q: 6.50 g of iron and 4.25 g of sulfur are heated: Fe(s) + S(s) → FeS(s). What mass of the excess reactant is left? (Fe 55.85 g/mol; S 32.06 g/mol)
h: Limiting reactant first; then mass of excess used; then subtract.
w: Fe is limiting. S used: 0.1164 mol × 32.06 g/mol = 3.73 g. Left: 4.25 g − 3.73 g = 0.52 g S.
x: 3.73 g is the sulfur that reacts. Subtract it from the 4.25 g present.
This subtracts the two masses (6.50 − 4.25). Iron and sulfur do not react gram for gram.
Iron is the limiting reactant, so no iron is left; the leftover is sulfur.

q: 6.60 g of propane and 20.0 g of O<sub>2</sub> react: C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>(g) + 5 O<sub>2</sub>(g) → 3 CO<sub>2</sub>(g) + 4 H<sub>2</sub>O(l). What is the maximum mass of CO<sub>2</sub>? (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> 44.097 g/mol; O<sub>2</sub> 31.998 g/mol; CO<sub>2</sub> 44.009 g/mol)
h: Each reactant → mol CO<sub>2</sub>. The smaller one wins.
w: O2 → 0.3750 mol CO2 (less than 0.4490 from propane), so O2 limits: 0.3750 × 44.009 = 16.5 g CO2.
x: This uses propane, the excess reactant. Propane is the smaller mass but not the limiting reactant.
This adds the reactant masses; the products include water, and some propane is left over.
This uses 3 CO<sub>2</sub> : 1 O<sub>2</sub>; the ratio is 3 CO<sub>2</sub> : 5 O<sub>2</sub>.

q: For 2 H<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) → 2 H<sub>2</sub>O(g), a student has 3.4 mol of H<sub>2</sub> and 2.0 mol of O<sub>2</sub> and says, “O<sub>2</sub> is limiting because there are fewer moles of it.” What is wrong with this reasoning?
c: Moles can be compared directly only when the coefficients are equal; here H<sub>2</sub> is limiting.
Nothing; the reactant with fewer moles is always limiting.
The student should compare grams instead of moles.
O<sub>2</sub> is limiting, but only because it has the larger molar mass.
h: How many moles of H<sub>2</sub> would 2.0 mol O<sub>2</sub> need?
w: H2 → 3.4 mol H2O; O2 → 4.0 mol H2O. H2 is limiting; compare moles only through the mole ratio.
x: That works only when the coefficients are equal. Here 2.0 mol O<sub>2</sub> needs 4.0 mol H<sub>2</sub>, and only 3.4 mol is present.
Comparing grams is even less reliable; molar masses differ.
O<sub>2</sub> is the excess reactant here, and molar mass does not decide which reactant limits.

q: For 2 SO2(g) + O2(g) → 2 SO3(g), which mixture in the table reacts with nothing left over?
h: The mixture must match the 2 : 1 ratio.
w: Only Mixture B (3.0 mol SO2 : 1.5 mol O2) is in the exact 2 : 1 ratio.
x: 2.0 mol SO<sub>2</sub> needs only 1.0 mol O<sub>2</sub>, so 1.0 mol O<sub>2</sub> is left.
1.0 mol SO<sub>2</sub> needs only 0.50 mol O<sub>2</sub>, so O<sub>2</sub> is left.
1.0 mol O<sub>2</sub> reacts with only 2.0 mol SO<sub>2</sub>, so SO<sub>2</sub> is left.

q: Burning 1.20 g of Mg, 2 Mg(s) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) → 2 MgO(s), gives 1.79 g of MgO. What is the percent yield? (Mg 24.31 g/mol; MgO 40.31 g/mol)
h: Find the theoretical yield of MgO first.
w: Theoretical = 1.990 g MgO; 1.79 g ÷ 1.990 g × 100% = 90.0%.
x: This divides theoretical by actual.
This compares the product with the mass of Mg. The theoretical yield of MgO is the right comparison.
This doubles the theoretical yield by multiplying the molar mass of MgO by its coefficient.

q: A student mixes 2.76 g of salicylic acid with 3.06 g of acetic anhydride, C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>3</sub> → C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>4</sub> + C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, and collects 2.95 g of aspirin. What is the percent yield? (C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>3</sub> 138.122 g/mol; C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>3</sub> 102.089 g/mol; C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>4</sub> 180.159 g/mol)
h: Which reactant is limiting? Only it sets the theoretical yield.
w: Salicylic acid limits; theoretical = 3.600 g aspirin. 2.95 ÷ 3.600 × 100% = 81.9%.
x: This takes the theoretical yield from acetic anhydride, the excess reactant, which makes the percent yield look too small.
This divides theoretical by actual.
This compares the aspirin with the mass of salicylic acid instead of with the theoretical yield.

q: A student filters alum crystals and weighs them right away, reporting a 106% yield. What is the most likely reason?
c: The crystals are still wet, so their mass includes water.
The reaction made more product than the limiting reactant allows.
Some crystals were lost in the filtrate.
The student used the limiting reactant to find the theoretical yield.
h: A yield above 100% means the product weighs more than it should. What could add mass?
w: A yield above 100% points to extra mass: here, water left in the crystals.
x: Matter is not created; no reaction can beat its theoretical yield.
Lost crystals lower the yield, not raise it.
Using the limiting reactant is the correct method; it does not cause a yield over 100%.

q: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 42.5 g. If the percent yield is 76.0%, what mass of product is collected?
h: Rearrange: actual = (percent ÷ 100) × theoretical.
w: Percent yield = (actual ÷ theoretical) × 100, so actual = 0.760 × 42.5 g = 32.3 g. The actual yield is always smaller than the theoretical yield when the percent is under 100%, so dividing by 0.760 (55.9 g) cannot be right.
x: This divides by 0.760, which gives more than the theoretical yield.
This multiplies by 76.0 without dividing by 100.
This is the mass that was not collected (24.0% of 42.5 g).

q: Ethanol for fuel is made by fermenting corn sugar: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> → 2 C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 2 CO<sub>2</sub>. From 64.0 g of glucose at an 82.0% yield, what mass of ethanol is collected? (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> 180.156 g/mol; C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH 46.069 g/mol)
h: Theoretical yield first, then take 82.0% of it.
w: Theoretical 32.73 g × 0.820 = 26.8 g C2H5OH.
x: This is the theoretical yield; the 82.0% has not been applied.
This divides by 0.820, which gives more than the theoretical yield.
This skips the mole ratio (each glucose makes 2 ethanol).

q: Hydrogen fuel cells run on 2 H<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) → 2 H<sub>2</sub>O(l), ΔH = −571.6 kJ. Which describes this reaction?
c: Exothermic: heat is released and the surroundings warm up
Endothermic: heat is absorbed and the surroundings cool down
Exothermic: heat is absorbed from the surroundings
Endothermic, because ΔH is a large number
h: Negative ΔH: released or absorbed?
w: ΔH < 0, so the reaction is exothermic: 571.6 kJ is released per 2 mol H2.
x: Endothermic reactions have a positive ΔH.
Exothermic means heat is released, not absorbed.
The sign, not the size, of ΔH tells you exo or endo.

q: Heating limestone is endothermic: CaCO<sub>3</sub>(s) → CaO(s) + CO<sub>2</sub>(g), ΔH = +178 kJ. What is ΔH for the reverse reaction, CaO(s) + CO<sub>2</sub>(g) → CaCO<sub>3</sub>(s)?
h: Reverse the equation, reverse the sign.
w: Reverse reaction: ΔH = −178 kJ (exothermic).
x: The reverse reaction releases the heat the forward one absorbs, so the sign changes.
Doubling would apply if the coefficients were doubled; they are not.
Halving would apply to half the amounts. Reversing changes only the sign.

q: Given 2 H<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) → 2 H<sub>2</sub>O(l), ΔH = −571.6 kJ, what is ΔH for 4 H<sub>2</sub>(g) + 2 O<sub>2</sub>(g) → 4 H<sub>2</sub>O(l)?
h: Double the equation, double ΔH.
w: 2 × (−571.6 kJ) = −1143.2 kJ.
x: ΔH belongs to the amounts as written; twice the amounts release twice the heat.
The reaction is still the same direction, so the sign stays negative.
This halves ΔH; the coefficients were doubled, not halved.

q: A Valley dairy digester burns captured methane, CH<sub>4</sub>(g) + 2 O<sub>2</sub>(g) → CO<sub>2</sub>(g) + 2 H<sub>2</sub>O(l), ΔH = −890.3 kJ. What mass of methane must burn to release 3.60 × 10<sup>4</sup> kJ? (CH<sub>4</sub> 16.043 g/mol)
h: Work backward: kJ → mol CH<sub>4</sub> → g CH<sub>4</sub>.
w: 3.60 × 104 kJ × (1 mol CH4 / 890.3 kJ) × (16.043 g / 1 mol) = 649 g CH4.
x: This stops at moles of methane.
This divides by the molar mass instead of multiplying.
This uses the coefficient of O<sub>2</sub> (2). The 890.3 kJ goes with 1 mol CH<sub>4</sub>.

q: A food label counts the energy in carbohydrates in Calories (1 Cal = 4.184 kJ). Using C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + 6 O<sub>2</sub> → 6 CO<sub>2</sub> + 6 H<sub>2</sub>O, ΔH = −2803 kJ, how many Calories does 12.0 g of glucose release? (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> 180.156 g/mol)
h: kJ first, then kJ → Cal.
w: 12.0 g × (1 mol / 180.156 g) × (2803 kJ / 1 mol) × (1 Cal / 4.184 kJ) = 44.6 Cal, about 3.7 Cal per gram.
x: This is the heat in kJ with a Cal label. Divide by 4.184 kJ/Cal.
This multiplies by 4.184; kJ → Cal means dividing, since a Calorie is bigger than a kJ.
This divides by 6, the coefficient of O<sub>2</sub>.

q: Decomposing limestone absorbs heat: CaCO<sub>3</sub>(s) → CaO(s) + CO<sub>2</sub>(g), ΔH = +178 kJ. How much heat is needed to decompose 35.0 g of CaCO<sub>3</sub>? (CaCO<sub>3</sub> 100.09 g/mol)
h: Positive ΔH: heat is needed. grams → moles → kJ.
w: 35.0 g × (1 mol / 100.09 g) × (178 kJ / 1 mol) = 62.2 kJ absorbed.
x: A positive ΔH means heat is absorbed, not released.
This multiplies grams by ΔH; convert to moles first.
This stops at moles; multiply by 178 kJ/mol.

q: Which of these is mainly kinetic energy?
c: Glycogen stored in a liver cell
Water held in Millerton Lake behind Friant Dam
h: Ask: is it moving right now?
w: Kinetic energy is energy of motion: flowing blood. The other three are stored (potential) energy.
x: Glycogen stores chemical potential energy in the arrangement of its atoms; it is released only when the body breaks it down.
A charged battery stores chemical potential energy until it is used.
Water held behind a dam has potential energy of position; it gains kinetic energy only when it is released and falls.

q: An air-activated hand warmer gets hot as iron powder inside reacts with oxygen. Which statement agrees with the law of conservation of energy?
c: Chemical potential energy of the reactants becomes heat; the total energy stays the same.
The reaction creates new energy, which is why the packet gets hot.
When the packet cools, its energy is destroyed.
The heat comes from the air, which loses all of its energy to the packet.
h: Energy can change form or move. Can it be made or destroyed?
w: The chemical potential energy becomes heat; total energy is conserved.
x: Energy is never created; the heat was stored as chemical potential energy in the reactants.
Energy is not destroyed when the packet cools; the heat moves into the surroundings and spreads out.
The air supplies oxygen, a reactant, but the heat comes from the reaction's stored chemical energy, not from the air's energy.

q: A cyclist eats a banana, then rides to the top of a hill and stops. Which sequence best describes the main energy changes?
c: Chemical potential energy (food) → kinetic energy of motion → potential energy of position at the top, plus heat
Kinetic energy (food) → chemical potential energy → kinetic energy at the top
Chemical potential energy (food) is used up and disappears as the cyclist climbs
Potential energy of position → chemical potential energy → heat
h: Start with the banana: is its energy stored or moving?
w: Chemical PE → kinetic energy → PE of position (+ heat). The total is conserved at every step.
x: Food holds stored (potential) energy, not kinetic energy, and the cyclist is stopped at the top.
Energy is not used up; it changes form into motion, energy of position, and heat.
The energy starts as chemical energy in the food, not as energy of position.

q: A large pot of soup and a teaspoon of the same soup are both at 70 °C. Which statement is correct?
c: They have the same average kinetic energy of particles, but the pot holds far more thermal energy and can release more heat.
The pot has the higher temperature because it holds more soup.
The teaspoon's particles have the higher average kinetic energy because there are fewer of them.
They hold the same amount of thermal energy because they are at the same temperature.
h: Temperature is an average. Thermal energy is a total.
w: Same temperature, same average KE; the pot has more particles, so more total thermal energy.
x: Both are at 70 °C. Amount does not change temperature.
The same temperature means the same average kinetic energy, whatever the number of particles.
The same temperature does not mean the same total energy. The pot has many more molecules, so it holds much more thermal energy.

q: A patient's temperature is 38.9 °C. What is it in degrees Fahrenheit?
w: °F = 1.8(38.9) + 32 = 102.0 °F, a fever. The 1.8 and 32 are exact; 1.8 × 38.9 = 70.0 (3 significant figures, 1 decimal place), and adding 32 keeps 1 decimal place.
x: This adds 32 before multiplying, 1.8(38.9 + 32). The formula multiplies the Celsius temperature by 1.8 first.
This divides by 1.8 instead of multiplying. A Fahrenheit degree is smaller, so the Fahrenheit number is larger.
This adds 273.15, which converts to kelvins, not to Fahrenheit.

q: A hiker rescued from a cold river has a core temperature of 93.2 °F, a sign of hypothermia. What is this in kelvins?
h: Two steps: °F → °C, then °C → K.
x: This leaves out the parentheses, so only 32 is divided by 1.8, before adding 273.15.
This stops at the Celsius value and labels it K. Add 273.15 to finish.
This subtracts 32 but never divides by 1.8, then adds 273.15.

q: Which statement about absolute zero is correct?
c: It is 0 K, or −273.15 °C, the lowest possible temperature; Kelvin temperatures are never negative.
It is 0 °C, the temperature at which water freezes.
It is −273.15 K, the coldest temperature ever measured.
It is 0 °F, so very cold objects can have negative Kelvin temperatures.
h: Where does the Kelvin scale start?
w: Absolute zero = 0 K = −273.15 °C, the lowest possible temperature.
x: 0 °C is the freezing point of water, which is 273.15 K, far above absolute zero.
Absolute zero is 0 K, which equals −273.15 °C. A temperature of −273.15 K is not possible.
0 °F is about −17.8 °C, not absolute zero; and Kelvin temperatures are never negative.

q: During an infection, a patient's temperature rises by 2.4 °C. By how many kelvins and how many Fahrenheit degrees did it rise?
h: This is a temperature change, not a temperature. Which offsets cancel?
w: Change in K = change in °C = 2.4 K; change in °F = 1.8 × 2.4 = 4.3 °F.
x: This converts 2.4 as if it were a temperature, adding 273.15 and 32. For a temperature change, those offsets cancel.
A Fahrenheit degree is smaller than a Celsius degree, so a change of 2.4 °C is more than 2.4 Fahrenheit degrees.
This divides by 1.8. A Celsius degree is larger, so the change in °F is a larger number, not a smaller one.

q: Four temperatures were recorded for four patients on different devices. Which is the highest temperature?
h: Convert all four to °C before you compare.
x: 38.1 °C is a fever, but one of the other readings converts to a higher Celsius value.
311.4 is the biggest number, but in kelvins it is 311.4 − 273.15 = 38.3 °C. Compare temperatures on the same scale.
(100.6 − 32) ÷ 1.8 = 38.1 °C, lower than another reading.

q: A large apple provides about 116 Cal (food Calories). How many kilojoules is this? (1 Cal = 4.184 kJ)
h: 1 Cal = 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ. Should the number of kJ be bigger or smaller than 116?
w: 116 Cal × (4.184 kJ / 1 Cal) = 485 kJ. 4.184 is exact, so the 3 significant figures of 116 set the answer.
x: This multiplies by 4184, which converts Calories to joules, and then labels the answer kJ.
This divides by 4.184, the conversion upside down; kJ should be a larger number than Cal.
This treats a food Calorie as a small calorie (1 cal = 4.184 J), giving joules and then kJ. A food Calorie is 1000 cal.

q: A hot-water bottle holds 955 g of water. As it cools from 52.5 °C to 37.0 °C, warming a patient's feet, what is q for the water? (c for water = 4.184 J/(g·°C))
h: ΔT = T<sub>final</sub> − T<sub>initial</sub>. Cooling: what sign?
w: q = (955 g)(4.184 J/(g·°C))(−15.5 °C) = −6.19 × 104 J; about 61.9 kJ is released. (Context only; follow device directions.)
x: This uses initial minus final. ΔT is final minus initial; cooling gives a negative ΔT and a negative q.
This is the answer in kJ labeled as J. q = mcΔT gives joules when c is in J/(g·°C).
This uses the final temperature, 37.0 °C, as ΔT. ΔT is the change, final minus initial.

q: A fluid warmer supplies 7.75 kJ of heat to warm a bag of saline from 18.5 °C to 37.0 °C. Treating the saline as water, what is its mass? (c = 4.184 J/(g·°C))
h: m = q / (cΔT), with q in joules.
w: m = 7750 J ÷ (4.184 × 18.5 °C) = 100. g. (Context only.)
x: This leaves q in kJ. Specific heat is in joules, so convert 7.75 kJ to 7750 J first.
This multiplies q by c. Solve q = mcΔT for m: m = q / (cΔT).
This uses the final temperature as ΔT. ΔT = 37.0 − 18.5.

q: A 52.4 g piece of jewelry absorbs 312 J as it warms from 22.6 °C to 47.9 °C. Use the table to identify the metal.
h: Calculate c = q / (mΔT), then find it in the table.
w: c = 312 J ÷ (52.4 g × 25.3 °C) = 0.235 J/(g·°C): silver.
x: Copper's specific heat is 0.385. The calculated value is much lower; check that ΔT = 47.9 − 22.6.
Iron's specific heat is 0.449, about twice the calculated value.
Aluminum's specific heat is 0.903, far higher than the calculated value.

q: A 65.0 g piece of iron at 99.2 °C is dropped into 45.0 g of water at 21.0 °C in a calorimeter. Both end at 31.5 °C. How much heat did the iron release? (c for water = 4.184 J/(g·°C))
h: Find the water's heat with q = mcΔT, then use −q<sub>hot</sub> = q<sub>cold</sub>.
w: qwater = (45.0 g)(4.184)(10.5 °C) = 1.98 × 103 J, so qiron = −1.98 × 103 J.
x: This is the water's q. The iron released that heat, so −q<sub>iron</sub> = q<sub>water</sub>: the iron's q is negative.
This uses the iron's mass (65.0 g) with water's specific heat. Use the water's own mass, 45.0 g.
This uses the final temperature, 31.5 °C, as the water's ΔT. The water warmed by 10.5 °C.

q: An 85.0 g metal block at 99.5 °C is placed in 45.0 g of water at 22.5 °C in a calorimeter. The final temperature of both is 33.9 °C. What is the specific heat of the metal? (c for water = 4.184 J/(g·°C))
h: Heat lost by the metal = heat gained by the water. Each one gets its own m and ΔT.
w: c = −(2.15 × 103 J) ÷ (85.0 g × −65.6 °C) = 0.385 J/(g·°C), copper.
x: This uses the final temperature, 33.9 °C, as the metal's ΔT.
This uses the water's mass for the metal. Use the metal's own mass, 85.0 g, with its own ΔT.
This uses the water's ΔT (11.4 °C) for the metal. The metal cooled by 65.6 °C.

q: How much heat is needed to melt 42.5 g of ice at 0 °C? (H<sub>2</sub>O 18.015 g/mol; ΔH<sub>fus</sub> = 6.02 kJ/mol)
h: q = nΔH<sub>fus</sub>. Grams to moles first.
x: This multiplies grams by kJ/mol. Convert grams to moles first, because ΔH<sub>fus</sub> is per mole.
This uses ΔH<sub>vap</sub> (40.7 kJ/mol). Melting uses the heat of fusion.
Melting absorbs heat (endothermic), so q is positive.

q: On the sloped segment of a heating curve where liquid water warms from 0 °C to 100 °C, which statement is correct?
c: The molecules speed up (kinetic energy rises), and q = mcΔT with c = 4.184 J/(g·°C).
The molecules move apart at constant temperature, and q = nΔH.
The molecules speed up, and q = mcΔT with c = 2.09 J/(g·°C).
No heat is absorbed, because the water does not change state.
h: Slope = temperature changing. Which state is warming?
w: Slope: KE rises; q = mcΔT with liquid water's c, 4.184 J/(g·°C).
x: That describes a plateau (phase change), where the temperature stays constant.
2.09 J/(g·°C) is the specific heat of ice. Each state has its own specific heat.
Heat is absorbed on every segment; on a slope it raises the temperature.

q: How much heat is needed to take 30.5 g of water at 64.0 °C to steam at 100 °C? (c for water = 4.184 J/(g·°C); ΔH<sub>vap</sub> = 40.7 kJ/mol; H<sub>2</sub>O 18.015 g/mol)
h: Two segments: a slope (mcΔT) and a plateau (nΔH). Put both in kJ, then add.
w: q1 = 4.59 kJ; q2 = 68.9 kJ; total = 73.5 kJ.
x: This is only the boiling step. The water must first be warmed from 64.0 °C to 100 °C.
This uses ΔH<sub>fus</sub> for the boiling step. Liquid to gas uses ΔH<sub>vap</sub>.
This multiplies grams by ΔH<sub>vap</sub> without converting to moles.

q: A 10.0 g ice cube at 0 °C absorbs 1.50 kJ of heat. What happens? (H<sub>2</sub>O 18.015 g/mol; ΔH<sub>fus</sub> = 6.02 kJ/mol; c<sub>water</sub> = 4.184 J/(g·°C); c<sub>ice</sub> = 2.09 J/(g·°C))
c: Only part of the ice melts, and the temperature stays at 0 °C.
All of the ice melts, and the water warms to 35.9 °C.
The ice warms to 71.8 °C without melting.
All of the ice melts, and the liquid water stays at 0 °C.
h: First find how much heat melting all of the ice would take. Is 1.50 kJ enough?
w: Melting needs 3.34 kJ > 1.50 kJ, so only part melts and the temperature stays at 0 °C.
x: This uses q = mcΔT as if the ice were already liquid. At 0 °C the heat first goes into melting.
Ice at 0 °C cannot warm above 0 °C until it has melted; this uses mcΔT for a phase change.
Melting all 10.0 g needs more heat than the 1.50 kJ supplied, so some ice is still left.

q: Chloroform, CHCl<sub>3</sub>, was once used as an anesthetic. It is a polar tetrahedral molecule. Which intermolecular forces act between chloroform molecules?
h: Polar? Then dipole–dipole. Any H on N, O, or F?
w: CHCl3: dispersion and dipole–dipole (no H on N, O, or F).
x: Dispersion only is for nonpolar molecules. With one H and three Cl, the bond dipoles do not cancel.
The H in CHCl<sub>3</sub> is bonded to carbon. Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded directly to N, O, or F.
Every molecule has dispersion forces, including polar ones.

q: Xenon (Xe) boils at a much higher temperature than neon (Ne), although both are nonpolar atoms. Why?
c: Xe has a much larger, more polarizable electron cloud, so its dispersion forces are stronger.
Xe is a heavier atom whose larger cloud makes it polar, so it has dipole–dipole forces.
Xe atoms in the liquid form hydrogen bonds with each other, the way water molecules do.
Xe forms weak covalent bonds with neighboring atoms when it condenses to a liquid.
h: What makes dispersion forces stronger?
w: Bigger electron cloud, more polarizable: stronger dispersion forces in Xe.
x: A single noble-gas atom has no permanent dipole, so it is nonpolar no matter how heavy it is.
Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded to N, O, or F, and there is no H here.
Noble gases in the liquid are held by intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds.

q: Potassium chloride, KCl, is added to many IV fluids. When it dissolves, which force holds water molecules around each K<sup>+</sup> ion?
c: Ion–dipole, with the δ− oxygen ends of water pointing toward K<sup>+</sup>
Ion–dipole, with the δ+ hydrogen ends of water pointing toward K<sup>+</sup>
Hydrogen bonding between K<sup>+</sup> and the H atoms of water
An ionic bond between K<sup>+</sup> and the O of water
h: Opposite partial charges attract. Which end of water is δ−?
w: Ion–dipole: water's δ− O ends surround K+; the δ+ H ends surround Cl−.
x: Like charges repel; the δ+ H ends point toward the negative Cl<sup>−</sup> ions, not toward K<sup>+</sup>.
Hydrogen bonds need H on N, O, or F and a lone pair on N, O, or F; K<sup>+</sup> has neither role.
Water stays a neutral molecule; the attraction is an intermolecular ion–dipole force, not an ionic bond.

q: When ethanol boils, what is overcome?
c: The intermolecular forces between ethanol molecules; each molecule stays intact
The covalent C–H bonds inside each molecule
The O–H covalent bonds, which break to release hydrogen gas
All the bonds, so the molecules split into separate atoms
h: Is boiling a physical or a chemical change?
w: Boiling overcomes intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds, dipole–dipole, dispersion); the molecules stay whole.
x: Covalent bonds within the molecule are much stronger than intermolecular forces and are not broken by boiling.
Ethanol vapor is ethanol; no hydrogen gas forms. Hydrogen bonds between molecules are overcome, not covalent O–H bonds.
Boiling is a physical change; the molecules keep their identity.

q: The two strands of DNA are held together by attractions between base pairs (A with T, G with C). What are these attractions, and why do they matter?
c: Hydrogen bonds between N–H groups and N or O atoms; each is weak, so the strands can unzip for copying
Covalent bonds between the bases; they are very strong, so the strands never separate
Ionic bonds between the bases, formed by transferring electrons
Dispersion forces only, because the bases are nonpolar
h: Look for H on N facing a lone pair on N or O.
w: Hydrogen bonds hold base pairs together: weak one at a time, strong in total.
x: The strands must separate to copy and read genes; covalent bonds would be far too strong for that.
No electrons are transferred between base pairs; they are attracted by hydrogen bonds.
The bases have polar N–H, N, and O groups, which form hydrogen bonds.

q: Which pair of atoms describes a hydrogen bond?
c: The H of one water molecule and the O of a neighboring water molecule
The H and the O within one water molecule
The H of one CH<sub>4</sub> molecule and the C of a neighboring CH<sub>4</sub> molecule
The H of one CH<sub>3</sub>F molecule and the F of a neighboring CH<sub>3</sub>F molecule
h: A hydrogen bond is an attraction between molecules, and the H must be bonded to N, O, or F.
w: H on one water molecule ··· O of another.
x: The O–H inside one molecule is a covalent bond, not a hydrogen bond.
C–H bonds are nonpolar by the Chapter 6 rule, and C has no lone pair; methane has dispersion forces only.
In CH<sub>3</sub>F every H is bonded to carbon, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself, even though F is present.

q: Which of these liquids has the highest surface tension?
h: Stronger intermolecular forces, higher surface tension.
w: Water: hydrogen bonding gives the strongest pull at the surface.
x: Acetone is polar but has no O–H, so it has dipole–dipole forces, weaker than water's hydrogen bonding.
Pentane is nonpolar, with dispersion forces only.
Dichloromethane is polar with no H on N, O, or F: dipole–dipole, weaker than hydrogen bonding.

q: Ethylene glycol, HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, is much more viscous than ethanol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH. What is the best explanation?
c: Each ethylene glycol molecule has two O–H groups, so it forms more hydrogen bonds with its neighbors.
Ethylene glycol is nonpolar, so its molecules slide past each other slowly.
Ethanol has stronger hydrogen bonding, which makes it flow faster.
Viscosity depends only on molar mass, and ethylene glycol is heavier.
h: Both hydrogen bond. Which molecule can make more of them?
w: Two O–H groups per molecule, more hydrogen bonds, higher viscosity.
x: Ethylene glycol is polar, with two O–H groups.
Stronger attractions make a liquid flow more slowly, not faster, and ethanol has fewer O–H groups.
Size matters, but the number of hydrogen bonds matters at least as much here; molar mass alone does not explain the large difference.

q: During a finger-stick blood test, blood rises on its own into a thin glass capillary tube. Why?
c: Blood is attracted to the glass (adhesion) more strongly than to itself (cohesion).
Blood is attracted to itself (cohesion) more strongly than to the glass (adhesion).
Blood has a high vapor pressure, so its vapor pushes it up the narrow tube.
Gravity pulls blood more strongly into a narrow tube than into a wide one.
h: Liquid-to-wall attraction versus liquid-to-liquid attraction.
w: Adhesion > cohesion, so the blood climbs the tube (capillary action).
x: When cohesion wins, the liquid pulls away from the walls and does not climb.
Vapor pressure is about molecules escaping into the gas phase, not climbing a tube.
Gravity pulls liquids down, and capillary action works against it.

q: Silicon carbide, SiC, used in grinding wheels and sandpaper, is extremely hard and does not melt even at 2000 °C. What type of solid is it?
h: Nonmetals only usually means molecular. Which few are the exceptions?
w: Covalent network, like diamond and quartz: covalent bonds throughout.
x: SiC is made of nonmetal-like elements, but it does not exist as separate small molecules; molecular solids are soft and melt low.
Si and C are both nonmetals or metalloids, with no metal cation, so SiC is not ionic.
SiC contains no metal and does not conduct or bend like a metal.

q: Which statement about solid sodium chloride (table salt) is correct?
c: It has a high melting point and is brittle, and it does not conduct electricity until it is melted or dissolved.
It conducts electricity as a solid, because it is made of ions.
It has a low melting point, because its particles are held by intermolecular forces.
It bends without breaking, like a metal.
h: Ions can carry charge only if they can move.
w: Ionic solids: high melting point, brittle, conduct only when melted or dissolved.
x: Ions are present, but in the solid they cannot move, so solid NaCl does not conduct.
NaCl is held by ionic bonds throughout the crystal, so it melts high (801 °C).
Ionic crystals are brittle: shifting a layer lines up like charges, which repel and crack the crystal.

q: At 25 °C, which of these liquids has the highest vapor pressure?
h: Weakest forces, highest vapor pressure. Compare the strongest force before size.
w: Pentane: the only liquid here without hydrogen bonding, so the highest vapor pressure (most volatile).
x: 1-Propanol hydrogen bonds through its O–H group, so it holds its molecules more tightly than a nonpolar liquid of similar size.
Water's extensive hydrogen bonding gives it a low vapor pressure, even though its molar mass is the smallest.
Acetic acid has an O–H group and hydrogen bonds strongly, so it evaporates slowly.

q: At a high Sierra Nevada campsite, water boils below 100 °C. Why?
c: The air pressure is lower, so water's vapor pressure reaches the outside pressure at a lower temperature.
The air pressure is higher, which lowers the boiling point.
Mountain water has fewer hydrogen bonds.
Boiling point does not depend on pressure; the thermometer is cold.
h: Boiling: vapor pressure = outside pressure.
w: Lower outside pressure, so water boils at a lower temperature, and food cooks more slowly.
x: Air pressure is lower at high altitude, and higher pressure would raise the boiling point.
Water is the same substance at any altitude; its hydrogen bonding is unchanged.
Boiling point depends on outside pressure; 100 °C is the normal boiling point at 1 atm.

q: An autoclave sterilizes surgical instruments with steam at about 121 °C. How can the water reach 121 °C?
c: The autoclave raises the pressure, which raises water's boiling point above 100 °C.
The autoclave lowers the pressure, which raises the boiling point.
Steam always has a temperature of 121 °C.
The autoclave adds heat faster than water can boil, so the boiling point rises.
h: What does a higher outside pressure do to the boiling point?
w: Higher pressure, higher boiling point: steam at 121 °C kills even heat-resistant spores.
x: Lower pressure lowers the boiling point, as at high altitude.
Steam can be at many temperatures; at 1 atm, water boils at 100 °C.
Heating faster makes water boil sooner, but the boiling temperature is set by the pressure.

q: To freeze-dry (lyophilize) a vaccine, the frozen sample is placed under very low pressure until the ice is gone. How is the ice removed?
c: By sublimation: the ice turns directly into water vapor, absorbing heat
By deposition: the ice turns directly into vapor, releasing heat
By melting the ice and then boiling the liquid
By condensation of the ice into vapor
h: Solid straight to gas: what is it called?
w: Sublimation (endothermic) removes the ice and leaves a dry product.
x: Deposition is the reverse, gas to solid, and it releases heat.
Freeze-drying skips the liquid; at very low pressure the ice goes straight to vapor.
Condensation is gas to liquid, which is not what happens to the ice.

q: The three substances in the table have nearly the same molar mass. Rank them from lowest to highest boiling point.
h: Similar size: rank by the strongest force in each.
w: Dispersion < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bond: butane < acetone < 1-propanol (about 0 °C, 56 °C, and 97 °C).
x: This ranks by molar mass. With sizes this close, the strongest force decides: acetone is polar, butane is not.
This is the order of vapor pressure, from highest boiling to lowest. The question asks for lowest to highest boiling point.
Acetone has dipole–dipole forces only; 1-propanol hydrogen bonds, so 1-propanol boils higher.

q: Rank from lowest to highest melting point: F2, HF, NaF, SiO2 (quartz).
h: Classify each solid, then use the strongest force, then size.
w: F2 < HF < NaF < SiO2: molecular (dispersion) < molecular (H bonds) < ionic < covalent network.
x: This ranks by molar mass (20 < 38 < 42 < 60). HF is the lightest, but its hydrogen bonds beat the dispersion forces of F<sub>2</sub>.
This treats SiO<sub>2</sub> as a small molecule. Quartz is a covalent network and melts near 1700 °C.
This puts hydrogen bonding above ionic bonding. Ionic solids such as NaF melt far higher than molecular solids.

q: Which property of gases shows most directly that a gas is mostly empty space?
c: A gas can be compressed into a much smaller volume.
A gas has a definite shape.
A gas is denser than the liquid it comes from.
Gas particles attract each other strongly.
h: What can you do to a tank of oxygen that you cannot do to a bottle of water?
w: Compressibility shows the empty space: a gas can be squeezed into a much smaller volume.
x: Gases have no definite shape; they take the shape of their container.
Gases are about a thousand times less dense than liquids, because their particles are so far apart.
In kinetic molecular theory, gas particles neither attract nor repel each other.

q: According to kinetic molecular theory, what causes the pressure a gas exerts on its container?
c: Gas particles colliding with the container walls
Gas particles attracting the walls of the container
The weight of the gas particles resting on the bottom of the container
Gas particles growing larger as they are heated
h: Think of the particles as tiny moving balls.
w: Pressure comes from particles colliding with the walls: more or harder hits, higher pressure.
x: KMT treats gas particles as neither attracting nor repelling anything; pressure comes from collisions.
Gas particles do not settle; they move constantly and hit every wall, including the top.
Particles do not change size when heated; they move faster.

q: A cylinder of carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>, 44.009 g/mol) and a cylinder of nitrogen (N<sub>2</sub>, 28.014 g/mol) stand side by side in a hospital supply room at 22 °C. How do the average kinetic energies of their molecules compare?
c: They are the same, because both gases are at the same temperature.
The CO<sub>2</sub> molecules have more, because they are heavier.
The N<sub>2</sub> molecules have more, because they move faster.
It cannot be compared without knowing the pressure in each cylinder.
h: What single variable sets the average kinetic energy?
w: Same temperature, so the same average kinetic energy; the lighter N2 molecules simply move faster.
x: Heavier molecules at the same temperature move more slowly; their average kinetic energy is the same as that of lighter ones.
The N<sub>2</sub> molecules are faster, but being lighter they carry the same average kinetic energy as the slower CO<sub>2</sub> molecules.
Pressure depends on how many particles hit the walls; the average kinetic energy per particle is set by temperature alone.

q: Cotton swabs soaked in ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>, 17.031 g/mol) and hydrochloric acid (HCl, 36.46 g/mol) are placed at opposite ends of a long glass tube at the same time. A white ring of NH<sub>4</sub>Cl forms where the two gases meet. Where does the ring form?
c: Closer to the HCl end, because NH<sub>3</sub> molecules move faster
Closer to the NH<sub>3</sub> end, because NH<sub>3</sub> molecules move faster
Exactly in the middle, because both gases have the same average kinetic energy
Closer to the HCl end, because HCl molecules move faster
h: Which gas is lighter, and so diffuses faster?
w: NH3 is lighter and diffuses faster, so it travels farther: the ring forms closer to the HCl end.
x: NH<sub>3</sub> is faster, so it covers more of the tube; the gases meet away from the NH<sub>3</sub> end.
Equal kinetic energy does not mean equal speed: the lighter molecules move faster.
HCl is the heavier gas, so it moves more slowly; the ring forms near its end because the NH<sub>3</sub> travels farther.

q: A sample of carbon dioxide gas starts at room temperature and 1 atm. Which change makes it depart more from ideal-gas behavior?
c: Cooling it toward the temperature where it condenses
Heating it to a higher temperature
Letting it expand into a larger container
h: When do attractions between particles start to matter?
w: Real gases depart from ideal behavior at low temperature and high pressure: cooling it toward condensation.
x: Faster particles make attractions less important, so the gas behaves more ideally.
Lower pressure spreads the particles out, so the gas behaves more ideally.
Expanding lowers the pressure and spreads the particles out, which makes the gas more ideal.

q: The tip of a syringe is sealed, and the plunger is pushed in at constant temperature. Why does the pressure of the trapped air rise?
c: The same number of particles hit a smaller wall area more often.
The particles move faster because they have less room.
The particles become larger when they are squeezed.
Squeezing the air makes the particles attract each other.
h: Speed stays the same at constant temperature. What changes?
w: Same particles, less room: more frequent collisions with the walls, so higher pressure.
x: At constant temperature the average speed does not change; only the number of hits on the walls does.
Particle size does not change; only the spaces between the particles shrink.
KMT treats gas particles as having no attractions; pressure comes from collisions.

q: A person wearing narrow high heels sinks into a soft lawn, but the same person in flat shoes does not. Why?
c: The same force is spread over a smaller area, so the pressure is greater.
The person weighs more in high heels.
Pressure depends only on force, so the heels must push harder.
A smaller area gives a smaller pressure, so the lawn is softer under heels.
h: Use P = F/A.
w: Same force, smaller area: greater pressure (P = F/A).
x: The person's weight, the force, is the same in either pair of shoes.
Pressure is force divided by area, so area matters as much as force.
A smaller area gives a greater pressure, not a smaller one.

q: In a mercury barometer, what holds up the column of mercury in the closed glass tube?
c: The atmosphere pushing down on the mercury in the open dish
Suction from the vacuum at the top of the tube
The mercury sticking to the glass walls
The weight of the mercury in the dish pushing up
h: Which side of the mercury has air on it?
w: Atmospheric pressure on the dish pushes the mercury up the tube until the column's weight balances it.
x: A vacuum exerts no pull. The column is pushed up from below by air pressure on the dish.
Mercury does not wet glass, and sticking could not hold up a 760 mm column.
The mercury in the dish is pushed on by the air; its own weight does not lift the column.

q: A hiker drinks from a plastic water bottle on the summit of Mount Whitney (14,505 ft), caps it tightly, and hikes down to Lone Pine (3,727 ft). The empty bottle is crumpled. Why?
c: The air pressure outside is greater at the lower elevation, so the outside air pushes the bottle in.
The air inside the bottle escaped through the cap on the way down.
The air pressure outside is lower at the lower elevation, so the bottle collapses.
The air inside the bottle got heavier at the lower elevation.
h: Is there more air above you at the summit or in the valley?
w: Lower elevation, more air above, higher outside pressure, which crushes the bottle sealed at the summit.
x: The cap was tight; the amount of air inside did not change.
Air pressure is higher at lower elevations, because there is more air above.
The mass of the trapped air does not change; the outside pressure does.

q: Some hospitals report blood gases in kilopascals. A patient's arterial carbon dioxide pressure is 41.5 mmHg. What is it in kPa?
h: Use 760 mmHg = 101.325 kPa (both equal 1 atm).
w: 41.5 mmHg × (101.325 kPa / 760 mmHg) = 5.53 kPa.
x: This multiplies mmHg by 101.325 as if the value were in atm. Convert mmHg to atm first (divide by 760).
This divides by 101.325 and never uses 760 mmHg = 1 atm.
This flips both conversion factors (× 760 ÷ 101.325). Check: 760 mmHg = 101.325 kPa, so the number of kPa must be smaller than the number of mmHg.

q: An air-filled balloon is moved from a warm room into a freezer. The pressure and the amount of air stay the same. What happens to the balloon's volume?
c: It decreases, because volume and Kelvin temperature are directly related.
It increases, because volume and temperature are inversely related.
It stays the same, because the amount of air does not change.
It decreases, because the pressure on the balloon increases.
h: Which law relates V and T, and is it direct or inverse?
w: Charles's law, direct: lower temperature, smaller volume.
x: Volume and temperature are directly related (Charles's law); cooling shrinks the gas.
The amount of air is constant, but the temperature drops, so the volume drops.
The pressure is constant here; the change comes from the temperature.

q: A rigid tank of gas (constant volume) has its amount of gas doubled, and at the same time its Kelvin temperature is doubled. What happens to the pressure?
h: Do each change separately: what does doubling n do? What does doubling T do?
w: ×2 for the moles and ×2 for the temperature: 4 times the pressure.
x: This counts only one of the two changes; each one doubles the pressure.
Both changes raise the pressure; neither one cancels the other.
More gas and hotter gas both mean more frequent, harder collisions, so the pressure goes up.

q: A 285 mL flask holds argon at 738 mmHg and 21.5 °C. How many moles of argon are in the flask?
h: Line up the units with R = 0.082058 L·atm/(mol·K).
x: This puts mmHg into PV = nRT with R = 0.082058, so the answer is 760 times too large.
This uses 285 mL as if it were liters, so the answer is 1000 times too large.
This uses the Celsius temperature; R needs kelvins.

q: What volume does 7.25 g of methane, CH<sub>4</sub> (16.043 g/mol), occupy at STP?
h: Our goal is the mole: g → mol → L.
w: 7.25 g ÷ 16.043 g/mol = 0.4519 mol; × 22.4 L/mol = 10.1 L.
x: This treats grams as moles. Convert to moles with the molar mass first.
This divides grams by 22.4 and never uses the molar mass.
This finds the moles and then divides by 22.4; moles times 22.4 L/mol gives liters.

q: A student uses 22.4 L/mol to find the volume of 1.00 mol of gas at 37 °C and 1 atm. How does the student's answer compare with the true volume?
c: It is too small, because a gas at 37 °C occupies more than 22.4 L per mole.
It is too large, because a gas at 37 °C occupies less than 22.4 L per mole.
It is correct, because 22.4 L/mol works for any gas.
It is correct, because the pressure is 1 atm.
h: STP is 0 °C and 1 atm. Is 37 °C warmer or colder?
w: At 37 °C, 1 mol occupies about 25.5 L, so 22.4 L is too small.
x: Warming a gas at constant pressure makes its volume larger, not smaller.
22.4 L/mol is the same for every ideal gas, but only at STP.
STP needs both 1 atm and 0 °C; the temperature here is 37 °C.

q: A 1.45 g sample of an unknown gas occupies 0.825 L at 1.05 atm and 27.5 °C. What is its molar mass?
h: Molar mass = grams ÷ moles; get the moles from PV = nRT.
x: This uses 27.5 °C in PV = nRT; convert to kelvins.
This divides moles by grams. Molar mass is grams per mole: M = m/n.
This is the density, mass divided by volume (g/L), not the molar mass.

q: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2 H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>(aq) → 2 H<sub>2</sub>O(l) + O<sub>2</sub>(g). What volume of O<sub>2</sub> at STP forms from 8.50 g of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> (34.014 g/mol)?
h: g → mol → mole ratio → L at STP.
w: 8.50 g ÷ 34.014 g/mol = 0.2499 mol H2O2; × ½ = 0.1249 mol O2; × 22.4 L/mol = 2.80 L.
x: This skips the mole ratio; 2 mol H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> give only 1 mol O<sub>2</sub>.
This flips the mole ratio (2/1 instead of 1/2).
This uses grams of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> as if they were moles.

q: Propane burns in a camp stove: C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>(g) + 5 O<sub>2</sub>(g) → 3 CO<sub>2</sub>(g) + 4 H<sub>2</sub>O(g). What volume of CO<sub>2</sub> at 0.975 atm and 27.5 °C forms from 3.65 g of C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> (44.097 g/mol)?
h: Not at STP: after the mole ratio, use V = nRT/P.
x: This uses 22.4 L/mol, which is only for STP. These conditions are not STP, so use V = nRT/P.
This skips the mole ratio and finds the volume of the propane's moles; each mole of propane makes 3 mol CO<sub>2</sub>.
This uses the Celsius temperature in V = nRT/P.

q: Ethane burns: 2 C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>(g) + 7 O<sub>2</sub>(g) → 4 CO<sub>2</sub>(g) + 6 H<sub>2</sub>O(g). What volume of water vapor forms when 3.20 L of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> burns, with both gases measured at the same temperature and pressure?
h: Same T and P: liters behave like moles.
w: At the same temperature and pressure, gas volumes react in the same ratio as moles, so the coefficients apply directly to liters. 3.20 L C2H6 × (6 L H2O / 2 L C2H6) = 9.60 L. Flipping the ratio to 2/6 gives 1.07 L, which is too small because the equation makes three times as much water vapor as ethane burned.
x: This flips the ratio (2/6 instead of 6/2).
This assumes a 1 : 1 ratio; the coefficients are 2 C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> : 6 H<sub>2</sub>O.
This multiplies by 6 but forgets to divide by the 2 in front of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>.

q: For 2 H<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) → 2 H<sub>2</sub>O(l), a student says, “4.0 L of H<sub>2</sub> makes 4.0 L of water, because the coefficients are 2 : 2.” What is wrong?
c: Volume ratios apply only to gases; the water here is a liquid.
Nothing; coefficients always give volume ratios.
The ratio should be 2 : 1, so 4.0 L of H<sub>2</sub> makes 2.0 L of water.
Volume ratios apply only at STP.
h: Look at the state symbol for water.
w: Volume ratios come from Avogadro's law, which is about gases: liquid water does not follow it.
x: Coefficients give volume ratios only for gases at the same temperature and pressure.
The 2 : 2 mole ratio is right; the problem is that water is a liquid, so moles do not convert to liters this way.
Volume ratios work at any temperature and pressure, as long as all the gases are at the same conditions.

q: An antacid tablet neutralizes stomach acid: CaCO<sub>3</sub>(s) + 2 HCl(aq) → CaCl<sub>2</sub>(aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O(l) + CO<sub>2</sub>(g). What volume of CO<sub>2</sub> at 0.988 atm and 37.0 °C forms from 0.750 g of CaCO<sub>3</sub> (100.09 g/mol)?
h: g → mol → 1 : 1 → V = nRT/P.
x: This uses 22.4 L/mol, but 37.0 °C is not STP.
This uses the Celsius temperature.
This uses the 2 from HCl; CaCO<sub>3</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub> are 1 : 1.

q: During dental sedation, a nitrous oxide–oxygen mixture is delivered at a total pressure of 1.02 atm. The mole fraction of N<sub>2</sub>O is 0.650. What is the partial pressure of N<sub>2</sub>O?
h: P<sub>i</sub> = X<sub>i</sub> × P<sub>total</sub>.
w: By Dalton's law, a gas's partial pressure is its mole fraction times the total pressure: 0.650 × 1.02 atm = 0.663 atm. A partial pressure can never be larger than the total, so dividing (1.57 atm) cannot be right. The value 0.357 atm belongs to O2, whose mole fraction is 0.350.
x: This divides the mole fraction by the total pressure; multiply them.
This divides the total by the mole fraction, which gives a partial pressure larger than the total.
This uses 1 − 0.650, the mole fraction of O<sub>2</sub>; it is the oxygen's partial pressure.

q: A student collects 48.5 mL of oxygen over water at 20.0 °C. The room pressure is 746 mmHg, and water's vapor pressure at 20.0 °C is 17.5 mmHg. How many moles of O<sub>2</sub> were collected?
h: Dry gas pressure first, then convert units to match R.
x: This uses the room pressure; subtract water's vapor pressure first, because only part of the pressure belongs to the O<sub>2</sub>.
This uses mmHg with R = 0.082058, so the answer is 760 times too large.
This adds the water vapor pressure; it should be subtracted.

q: On the summit of Mount Whitney the air pressure is about 438 mmHg. Use the composition of dry air in the table. What is the partial pressure of oxygen on the summit?
h: P<sub>O2</sub> = X<sub>O2</sub> × P<sub>total</sub>; X = percent ÷ 100.
w: 0.2095 × 438 mmHg = 91.8 mmHg, much lower than at sea level, which is why breathing is harder at altitude.
x: This uses 20.95 without dividing by 100.
This uses sea-level pressure, 760 mmHg. On the summit the total pressure is 438 mmHg.
This divides by the mole fraction; multiply by it.

q: Why must water's vapor pressure be subtracted from the room pressure when a gas is collected over water?
c: The gas in the tube is a mixture of the collected gas and water vapor, and together they balance the room pressure.
Water vapor is heavier than the collected gas, so it pushes down on the tube.
The water absorbs some of the gas, lowering its pressure.
The room pressure must be converted to the pressure of liquid water.
h: What else, besides the collected gas, is in the tube?
w: The tube holds gas plus water vapor; Dalton's law says their pressures add to Patm.
x: Weight is not the reason; each gas in a mixture contributes its own partial pressure.
The correction is for water vapor added to the gas, not gas lost into the water.
Liquid water does not have a 'pressure' to convert to; its vapor contributes a partial pressure.

q: Helium is pumped into a rigid tank that already contains oxygen, at constant temperature. What happens to the partial pressure of the oxygen?
c: It stays the same, while the total pressure increases.
It decreases, because the helium pushes the oxygen aside.
It increases, because the total pressure increases.
It decreases, because the mole fraction of oxygen decreases while the total pressure stays the same.
h: Each gas behaves as if it were alone in the tank.
w: Oxygen's moles, V, and T are unchanged, so its partial pressure stays the same; the total rises.
x: Gas particles in KMT do not push each other aside; oxygen's pressure depends only on its own moles, V, and T.
The total rises because helium adds its own partial pressure; oxygen's share in pressure units does not change.
Oxygen's mole fraction does fall, but the total pressure rises by just enough that X × P<sub>total</sub> stays the same.

q: Mateo Herrera, who has asthma, is on supplemental oxygen, and the air he breathes in has an O<sub>2</sub> mole fraction of about 0.285. In his airways it is warmed to 37.0 °C and saturated with water vapor (47.1 mmHg). If the air pressure is 758 mmHg, what is the partial pressure of O<sub>2</sub> in the humidified air?
h: Subtract water vapor first, then multiply by the mole fraction.
x: This forgets the water vapor. Humidified air in the airways includes water vapor at 47.1 mmHg.
This adds the water vapor instead of subtracting it.
This uses 1 − 0.285, the share of the other gases, not oxygen's share.

q: A hand sanitizer gel is 62% ethanol and 38% water by volume. Which component is the solvent?
c: Ethanol, because it is present in the larger amount
Water, because water is always the solvent
The gelling agent, because it holds the mixture together
Neither; a gel cannot contain a solution
h: The solvent is whichever component there is more of.
w: 62% is more than 38%, so ethanol is the solvent and water is the solute.
x: Water is the most common solvent, but here there is less water (38%) than ethanol (62%).
The gelling agent is a small additive; the solvent is the component present in the largest amount.
The liquid in the gel is a homogeneous mixture of ethanol and water, which is a solution.

q: Which pair of liquids is immiscible (forms two layers)?
h: Immiscible liquids are unlike: one polar, one nonpolar.
w: Polar water and nonpolar hexane do not mix: water and hexane.
x: Ethanol's O–H group hydrogen bonds with water, so the two are miscible.
Acetone is polar and accepts hydrogen bonds from water, so the two mix in all proportions.
Both are nonpolar hydrocarbons with dispersion forces only; like dissolves like, so they mix.

q: The solubility of sucrose is 204 g per 100 g of water at 20 °C. A candy maker dissolves 110. g of sucrose in 50.0 g of hot water, then cools it carefully to 20 °C without any crystals forming. How is the solution described at 20 °C?
c: Not a solution, because there is more sugar than water
h: Scale the solubility to 50.0 g of water first.
w: Capacity at 20 °C: 204 g × 50.0/100 = 102 g. 110. g > 102 g: supersaturated.
x: This compares 110. g with 204 g, but 204 g is for 100 g of water. Only 50.0 g of water was used.
A saturated solution holds exactly the maximum, 102 g in 50.0 g of water. This one holds more.
A solution can contain more solute than solvent by mass; the sugar is dissolved, so it is a homogeneous mixture.

q: A crystal of sugar is dropped into a saturated sugar solution at constant temperature. What happens?
c: The crystal stays undissolved, and the amount dissolved does not change.
The crystal dissolves, because sugar is soluble in water.
Extra sugar crystallizes out of the solution onto the crystal.
h: Saturated means the solution holds the maximum.
w: Saturated: the crystal stays undissolved.
x: That would happen in an unsaturated solution. A saturated one cannot hold any more.
That happens when a seed crystal is added to a supersaturated solution.
Adding solid to a saturated solution does not push more into solution; the extra stays undissolved.

q: Vitamin D is a large molecule made mostly of carbon and hydrogen, with only one O–H group. Where in the body does it dissolve best?
c: In fat (adipose) tissue, because both are mostly nonpolar
In blood plasma, because plasma is mostly water
In urine, because the kidneys filter it out
In stomach acid, because acids dissolve all molecules
h: One O–H on a big hydrocarbon frame: is the molecule mostly polar or nonpolar?
w: Mostly nonpolar, so it dissolves in fat (a fat-soluble vitamin).
x: Plasma is mostly polar water; a mostly nonpolar molecule dissolves poorly in it.
Water-soluble (polar) vitamins are excreted in urine; fat-soluble ones are stored instead.
Stomach acid is mostly water; it does not dissolve nonpolar molecules well.

q: Plasma dissolves about 4.35 mg of O<sub>2</sub> per liter when the O<sub>2</sub> partial pressure in the alveoli is 0.132 atm. In a hyperbaric chamber the O<sub>2</sub> partial pressure is raised to 2.45 atm at the same body temperature. What dissolved O<sub>2</sub> concentration does Henry's law predict?
h: Henry's law is direct: S<sub>1</sub>/P<sub>1</sub> = S<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>2</sub>.
w: S2 = 4.35 mg/L × 2.45 atm / 0.132 atm = 80.7 mg/L.
x: This inverts Henry's law; higher pressure means more dissolved gas, not less.
This multiplies by P<sub>2</sub> but never divides by P<sub>1</sub> = 0.132 atm.
Gas solubility depends on the gas's partial pressure; it does not stay the same.

q: A scuba diver rises to the surface too quickly. Why can nitrogen bubbles form in the diver's blood?
c: The pressure drops, so less N<sub>2</sub> can stay dissolved, and the extra comes out of solution as bubbles.
The pressure drops, so more N<sub>2</sub> dissolves until the blood is supersaturated with it.
The water near the surface is warmer, which makes N<sub>2</sub> more soluble in blood.
N<sub>2</sub> reacts with the blood at low pressure to form a new gas.
h: What happens to the pressure as the diver rises, and how does that affect a gas's solubility?
w: Less pressure, less dissolved gas: N2 comes out of solution as bubbles.
x: This reverses Henry's law: lower pressure means less gas can dissolve.
Warmer liquids hold less gas, and the main change on rising is the pressure.
N<sub>2</sub> is unreactive in the body; the bubbles are simply N<sub>2</sub> coming out of solution.

q: The solubility of KBr is 94.9 g per 100. g of water at 80.0 °C and 65.3 g per 100. g at 20.0 °C. A saturated solution made with 75.0 g of water at 80.0 °C is cooled to 20.0 °C. What mass of KBr crystallizes?
h: Scale both solubilities to 75.0 g of water, then subtract.
x: This is the difference for 100. g of water. The solution was made with only 75.0 g of water.
This is all the KBr dissolved at 80.0 °C; part of it can stay dissolved at 20.0 °C.
This is the KBr that stays dissolved at 20.0 °C, not the amount that comes out.

q: A sealed solution of NaCl in water is put under 5 atm of pressure at constant temperature. What happens to the solubility of the NaCl?
c: Almost nothing; pressure affects the solubility of gases, not solids.
It rises five times, by Henry's law.
It falls, because the pressure squeezes ions out of solution.
It rises, because pressure works like heating.
h: Henry's law is about which kind of solute?
w: Pressure matters only for gases: NaCl's solubility hardly changes.
x: Henry's law applies to gases dissolving in liquids, not to solids such as NaCl.
Pressure does not push dissolved ions out; it has almost no effect on solids.
Pressure is not the same as heating; at constant temperature it does not change a solid's solubility.

q: A tap-water sample contains 0.845 mg of fluoride in 1.25 L. What is the fluoride concentration in ppm?
h: 1 ppm ≈ 1 mg/L in dilute water.
x: This multiplies by 1000, as if converting mg to μg; that would give ppb, not ppm.
This divides liters by milligrams; the solute goes on top.
This ignores the volume. ppm ≈ mg per liter, so divide by 1.25 L.

q: A rural Valley well contains 0.00865 mg of arsenic per liter. What is this concentration in ppb?
h: Convert mg/L to μg/L.
x: This multiplies by 10<sup>6</sup>, which converts mg to ng and gives ppt, not ppb.
This divides by 1000; going from mg to the smaller μg makes the number larger.
0.00865 mg/L is the value in ppm. ppb needs μg/L.

q: A household bleach is 6.00% (m/m) sodium hypochlorite, NaOCl (74.44 g/mol), and has a density of 1.08 g/mL. What is the molarity of NaOCl?
h: Assume 100. g of solution: the percent gives grams of solute, and the density gives the volume.
w: Take 100. g of bleach: it holds 6.00 g NaOCl, or 6.00 g ÷ 74.44 g/mol = 0.08060 mol. Its volume is 100. g ÷ 1.08 g/mL = 92.59 mL = 0.09259 L. Molarity = 0.08060 mol ÷ 0.09259 L = 0.870 M. Treating the 100. g as 100. mL skips the density and gives 0.806 M.
x: This takes 100. g of solution as 100. mL. Use the density to find the volume.
This multiplies by the density (100 × 1.08 mL). Volume = mass ÷ density.
This uses grams of NaOCl instead of moles.

q: An IV bag is labeled 0.9% (m/v) NaCl. What does the label mean?
c: 0.9 g of NaCl in every 100 mL of solution
0.9 g of NaCl in every 100 g of water
0.9 g of NaCl added to every 100 mL of water
0.9 mol of NaCl in every liter of solution
h: m/v = mass of solute over volume of solution.
w: Percent (m/v) means grams of solute per 100 mL of solution, so the label means 0.9 g NaCl in every 100 mL of solution. The 100 mL is the final solution volume, not the water the salt is added to. Moles per liter would be molarity, not a percent.
x: That describes a mass percent based on the water only; %(m/v) uses mL of solution.
The denominator is the volume of solution, not the volume of water the salt is added to.
Moles per liter is molarity; a percent uses grams.

q: A student adds 0.175 mol of KCl to 1.000 L of water and stirs until it dissolves. Why is the molarity not exactly 0.175 M?
c: Molarity uses liters of solution, and the solution's volume is not exactly 1.000 L.
Molarity uses kilograms of solvent, not liters.
KCl separates into two ions, so the molarity doubles.
The moles of KCl decrease as it dissolves.
h: Look at the denominator of molarity.
w: M = mol / L of solution, and the solution is not exactly 1.000 L.
x: Kilograms of solvent is molality, not molarity.
Molarity counts formula units of KCl; counting ions matters for colligative properties, not for the molarity of KCl.
Dissolving does not destroy any KCl; the moles are unchanged.

q: A 16.0 mL sample of 0.880 M KCl is to be diluted to 0.275 M. How much water must be added?
h: M<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = M<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub> gives the total volume. Then subtract.
x: This is the total final volume V<sub>2</sub>, which already includes the 16.0 mL of stock.
This inverts the ratio; the volume must grow when the solution is diluted.
This adds the stock volume to V<sub>2</sub>; V<sub>2</sub> is already the total.

q: A urine culture has about 4.2 × 10<sup>6</sup> bacteria per mL. A technician adds 0.50 mL of it to 4.5 mL of sterile saline and mixes, then adds 0.50 mL of that tube to another 4.5 mL of saline (two dilutions in all). What is the concentration in the second tube?
h: Each 0.50 mL + 4.5 mL step is a 1-to-10 dilution; the factors multiply.
w: 4.2 × 106 ÷ 100 = 4.2 × 104 bacteria/mL.
x: This divides by 9 each time, using the saline added as V<sub>2</sub>. The total volume is 5.0 mL, so each factor is 10.
This counts only one dilution; there were two.
This divides by 10 + 10 = 20. Dilution factors multiply: 10 × 10.

q: When a solution is diluted with water, which quantity stays the same?
h: M × V = moles. What does M<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = M<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub> say stays fixed?
w: Moles of solute are unchanged by dilution.
x: The molarity goes down; that is the point of diluting.
The volume goes up as solvent is added.
Added water adds mass, so the mass of solution increases.

q: A 5.00 mL blood sample has a glucose concentration of 5.6 mM. How many moles of glucose does it contain?
h: Convert both: mM → M and mL → L.
x: This uses 5.6 mM as if it were 5.6 M; divide by 1000 first.
This multiplies mM by mL with neither converted.
This divides by 1000 one time too many.

q: What volume of 0.185 M KI reacts completely with 21.5 mL of 0.135 M Pb(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>? Pb(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>(aq) + 2 KI(aq) → PbI<sub>2</sub>(s) + 2 KNO<sub>3</sub>(aq)
h: V × M → mol → mole ratio → mol → ÷ M.
x: This skips the mole ratio. Each Pb(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> needs 2 KI.
This flips the mole ratio (1/2 instead of 2/1).
This multiplies moles of KI by the molarity; V = mol ÷ M.

q: Calcium carbonate, the scale that builds up in Valley pipes with hard water, can be made by precipitation. What mass of CaCO<sub>3</sub> (100.09 g/mol) forms when 35.0 mL of 0.0860 M CaCl<sub>2</sub> reacts with excess Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>? CaCl<sub>2</sub>(aq) + Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>(aq) → CaCO<sub>3</sub>(s) + 2 NaCl(aq)
h: V × M → mol CaCl<sub>2</sub> → mol CaCO<sub>3</sub> → g.
x: This uses mL as liters; convert 35.0 mL to 0.0350 L.
This is moles of CaCO<sub>3</sub>; multiply by the molar mass.
This divides by the molar mass; going from moles to grams, multiply.

q: To standardize a NaOH solution, a student dissolves 0.1715 g of oxalic acid, H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (90.034 g/mol), in water and titrates it with the NaOH. The endpoint takes 27.33 mL. What is the molarity of the NaOH? H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(aq) + 2 NaOH(aq) → Na<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(aq) + 2 H<sub>2</sub>O(l)
h: Solid known: grams → mol acid → mol NaOH (× 2) → ÷ L NaOH.
x: This treats the reaction as 1 : 1. Oxalic acid has two acidic hydrogens, so it needs 2 NaOH.
This flips the mole ratio: 2 mol NaOH per 1 mol H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>, so multiply by 2.
This uses grams of oxalic acid as moles; convert with the molar mass first.

q: A 0.4250 g sample of a crushed aspirin tablet is dissolved and titrated with 0.1185 M NaOH; the endpoint takes 18.54 mL. Aspirin, C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (180.159 g/mol), reacts 1 : 1 with NaOH. What is the mass percent of aspirin in the sample? C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaC<sub>9</sub>H<sub>7</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O(l)
h: Find grams of aspirin, then divide by the sample mass.
x: This divides moles by grams; convert moles of aspirin to grams first.
This is the mass of aspirin; the question asks for the percent of the sample.
This divides the sample mass by the aspirin mass; the part goes on top.

q: A chewable antacid tablet contains 0.610 g of calcium carbonate, CaCO<sub>3</sub> (100.09 g/mol). What volume of 0.105 M HCl, about the strength of stomach acid, can it neutralize? CaCO<sub>3</sub>(s) + 2 HCl(aq) → CaCl<sub>2</sub>(aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O(l) + CO<sub>2</sub>(g)
h: g → mol base → mol HCl (× 2) → L → mL.
w: 0.01219 mol HCl ÷ 0.105 M = 116 mL.
x: This skips the mole ratio; each CaCO<sub>3</sub> neutralizes 2 HCl.
This uses grams of CaCO<sub>3</sub> as moles; convert with the molar mass.
This flips the mole ratio; there are 2 mol HCl per mol CaCO<sub>3</sub>.

q: Equal volumes of 0.10 M HCl and 0.10 M H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> are each titrated with the same NaOH solution. How do the volumes of NaOH compare?
c: The H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> needs twice as much NaOH as the HCl.
Both need the same volume of NaOH.
The HCl needs twice as much NaOH as the H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.
The H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> needs half as much NaOH, because it is a stronger acid.
h: Write both balanced equations and compare the mole ratios.
w: Same moles of acid; H2SO4 reacts 1 : 2 with NaOH: twice as much NaOH.
x: Same moles of acid, but H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> has two acidic hydrogens; the mole ratio is not the same.
This reverses the two acids: it is H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> that gives two H<sup>+</sup>.
Each H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> gives two H<sup>+</sup>, so it needs more NaOH, not less.

q: Which solute has a van 't Hoff factor of i = 3 in water (assuming complete dissociation)?
h: Write the dissociation and count the ions.
w: Na2SO4 gives 2 Na+ + 1 SO42− = 3 particles.
x: KBr → K<sup>+</sup> + Br<sup>−</sup>: two particles (i = 2).
AlCl<sub>3</sub> → Al<sup>3+</sup> + 3 Cl<sup>−</sup>: four particles (i = 4).
Glucose is a nonelectrolyte and stays as one molecule (i = 1).

q: What is the freezing point of a 0.425 m KBr solution in water? (K<sub>f</sub> = 1.86 °C/m)
h: ΔT<sub>f</sub> = iK<sub>f</sub>m; subtract from 0.00 °C.
w: ΔTf = 1.58 °C; Tf = −1.58 °C.
x: This adds ΔTf to the freezing point. Dissolved particles lower the freezing point.
This forgets i. KBr gives two particles, K<sup>+</sup> and Br<sup>−</sup>.
This uses K<sub>b</sub> = 0.512, the boiling point constant. Use K<sub>f</sub> = 1.86 for freezing.

q: A membrane that lets only water pass separates 5% glucose (side A) from 10% glucose (side B). Which way does water flow by osmosis?
c: From side A to side B, toward the higher solute concentration
From side B to side A, toward the lower solute concentration
Glucose moves from side B to side A until both are 7.5%
No water moves, because both sides contain glucose
h: Water follows solute.
w: Water moves toward the more concentrated side: from A to B.
x: This reverses osmosis. Water moves toward the side with more dissolved particles.
The membrane blocks glucose; only water can cross.
Water moves whenever the particle concentrations differ; here they do.

q: In the emergency department, Mateo Herrera, who has asthma, receives 0.9% NaCl (normal saline) by IV. Relative to his red blood cells, how is this fluid described?
c: Isotonic: no net water flow, so the cells keep their shape
Hypotonic: water flows into the cells, and they swell
Hypertonic: water flows out of the cells, and they shrink
Hypertonic: water flows into the cells, and they burst
h: Compare 0.9% NaCl with the particle concentration inside red blood cells.
w: 0.9% NaCl is isotonic: no net water flow.
x: Hypotonic fluids, such as 0.45% NaCl, have a lower particle concentration than cells; 0.9% NaCl matches them.
Hypertonic fluids, such as 3% NaCl, have a higher particle concentration than cells.
In a hypertonic fluid water flows out of cells; and 0.9% NaCl is not hypertonic.

q: A solution is made by dissolving 1.45 g of MgCl<sub>2</sub> (95.21 g/mol) in 125.0 g of water. What is its osmolality in mOsm/kg, assuming complete dissociation?
h: Molality first, then × i, then × 1000 mOsm/Osm.
x: This forgets i; MgCl<sub>2</sub> gives Mg<sup>2+</sup> + 2 Cl<sup>−</sup>, three particles.
This uses i = 2; MgCl<sub>2</sub> gives three ions, not two.
This is the answer in Osm/kg; multiply by 1000 mOsm/Osm.

q: Highway crews spread NaCl on the road to Shaver Lake. What molality of NaCl solution freezes at −5.00 °C, assuming complete dissociation? (K<sub>f</sub> = 1.86 °C/m)
h: Solve ΔT<sub>f</sub> = iK<sub>f</sub>m for m.
w: NaCl dissociates into Na+ and Cl−, so i = 2. Solve ΔTf = iKfm for m: m = 5.00 ÷ (2 × 1.86) = 1.34 m. Leaving out i gives 2.69 m, twice the molality actually needed.
x: This forgets i; each NaCl gives two particles, so half this molality is enough.
This uses K<sub>b</sub> = 0.512; freezing point depression uses K<sub>f</sub> = 1.86.
This multiplies by iK<sub>f</sub>; solve ΔT<sub>f</sub> = iK<sub>f</sub>m for m by dividing.

q: A few drops of phenolphthalein are added to a clear solution, and it stays colorless. What can you conclude?
c: The solution is acidic or neutral.
The solution must be pure water.
h: Phenolphthalein: “pink means base.” What does colorless rule out?
w: Colorless rules out only a base: the solution is acidic or neutral.
x: A basic solution would turn phenolphthalein pink.
Neutral water also leaves phenolphthalein colorless, so acid is possible but not certain.
Any acidic solution would also leave it colorless; this test cannot single out pure water.

q: Iron filings are dropped into hydrochloric acid, and bubbles form as the iron dissolves. Iron forms Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions. What are the products?
h: Acid + active metal gives a salt and which gas?
w: Fe(s) + 2 HCl(aq) → FeCl2(aq) + H2(g): the bubbles are hydrogen gas, and the salt is FeCl2.
x: Water forms when an acid reacts with a base; there is no oxygen in the reactants here.
Carbon dioxide forms only when an acid reacts with a carbonate or bicarbonate.
An acid does not make a hydroxide or chlorine gas with a metal; the H<sup>+</sup> becomes H<sub>2</sub> gas.

q: In buttermilk pancakes, baking soda (NaHCO<sub>3</sub>) reacts with the lactic acid (HC<sub>3</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) in the buttermilk, and the batter puffs up. Which set of products is correct?
h: Acid + carbonate or bicarbonate gives a salt, water, and a gas.
w: NaHCO3(s) + HC3H5O3(aq) → NaC3H5O3(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g): sodium lactate, H2O, and CO2 (the gas that puffs the batter).
x: H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> forms first, but it breaks down into H<sub>2</sub>O and CO<sub>2</sub>; write those instead.
Hydrogen gas comes from an acid reacting with an active metal, not with a bicarbonate.
An acid does not make a hydroxide; the bicarbonate takes the acid's H<sup>+</sup> and gives off CO<sub>2</sub>.

q: Hydrobromic acid is neutralized by lithium hydroxide. What is the net ionic equation?
h: Strong acid + strong base: cross out the spectator ions.
w: Spectators Li+ and Br− drop out: H+(aq) + OH−(aq) → H2O(l).
x: This is the molecular equation. The net ionic equation leaves out the spectator ions.
Li<sup>+</sup> and Br<sup>−</sup> are spectator ions; they stay dissolved and do not react.
HBr is a strong acid and stays fully ionized; the H<sup>+</sup> reacts with OH<sup>−</sup> instead.

q: Pure water barely conducts electricity, but hydrochloric acid conducts well. Why?
c: HCl forms ions (H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup>) that carry charge through the solution.
HCl molecules are polar, and polar molecules carry current.
HCl contains hydrogen, which conducts like a metal.
HCl releases free electrons into the water.
h: What has to be present for a solution to conduct?
w: HCl ionizes into H3O+ and Cl− ions, which carry charge.
x: Polar molecules without charge, such as water itself, carry almost no current; ions are needed.
Hydrogen is a nonmetal; conduction in a solution comes from dissolved ions.
Solutions conduct by moving ions, not by free electrons.

q: Milk of magnesia, Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>, neutralizes stomach acid (HCl). In the balanced equation, how many water molecules form for each Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>?
h: The number of waters equals the number of H<sup>+</sup> (or OH<sup>−</sup>) that react.
w: Mg(OH)2(s) + 2 HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + 2 H2O(l): 2 waters.
x: One water would use only one of the two OH<sup>−</sup> ions in Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>.
This counts H atoms instead of water molecules.
A neutralization always makes water: H<sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>−</sup> → H<sub>2</sub>O.

q: Ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, neutralizes acids, yet it contains no hydroxide ion. Which definition explains why NH<sub>3</sub> is a base?
c: Brønsted–Lowry: NH<sub>3</sub> accepts a proton and becomes NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>.
Arrhenius: NH<sub>3</sub> releases OH<sup>−</sup> from its formula.
Brønsted–Lowry: NH<sub>3</sub> donates one of its three H atoms.
Arrhenius: NH<sub>3</sub> releases H<sup>+</sup> in water.
h: Does ammonia gain or lose an H when it reacts with water?
w: NH3 gains H+ to form NH4+: a Brønsted–Lowry base (proton acceptor).
x: NH<sub>3</sub> has no OH in its formula; the OH<sup>−</sup> comes from the water that lost a proton.
Donating H<sup>+</sup> would make NH<sub>3</sub> an acid. Ammonia gains an H instead.
Releasing H<sup>+</sup> describes an Arrhenius acid.

q:
In this reaction, which reactant is the Brønsted–Lowry base?
HC2H3O2(aq) + NH3(aq) ⇄ NH4+(aq) + C2H3O2−(aq)
h: The base is the reactant that gains an H from left to right.
w: NH3 becomes NH4+: NH3 accepts the proton.
x: Acetic acid loses an H<sup>+</sup> (it becomes acetate), so it is the acid.
NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> is a product: it is the conjugate acid of NH<sub>3</sub>.
Acetate is a product: it is the conjugate base of acetic acid.

q:
Dihydrogen phosphate reacts with water as shown. Which choice lists one of its two conjugate acid–base pairs?
H2PO4−(aq) + H2O(l) ⇄ HPO42−(aq) + H3O+(aq)
h: Pair each reactant with the product that differs from it by one H<sup>+</sup>.
w: H2PO4− loses H+ to become HPO42−: H2PO4−/HPO42− (the other pair is H2O/H3O+).
x: These are the two reactants (the acid and the base); a pair is a reactant with its product partner.
H<sub>2</sub>O pairs with H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, not with HPO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>; they differ by more than one H<sup>+</sup>.
These are the two products; each pairs with a reactant.

q: What is the conjugate acid of the carbonate ion, CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>?
h: Add one H and raise the charge by one.
w: A conjugate acid has one more H+ than its base: CO32− + H+ → HCO3−. Adding H+ adds one H and raises the charge by 1, from 2− to 1−. H2CO3 has two added H+, one step too far.
x: This adds two H<sup>+</sup>; H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> would be the conjugate acid of bicarbonate, one step further.
This adds the H but leaves the charge at 2−; adding H<sup>+</sup> raises the charge by 1.
This changes the charge without adding the H atom.

q: In which reaction does water act as a Brønsted–Lowry acid?
h: Water is the acid when it turns into OH<sup>−</sup>.
w: Only in the cyanide reaction does water lose H+ (to become OH−): CN−(aq) + H2O(l) ⇄ HCN(aq) + OH−(aq).
x: Here water gains H<sup>+</sup> and becomes H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, so it is the base.
Water accepts the proton from HClO<sub>4</sub> (it becomes H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>), so it is the base.
Water accepts the proton from HNO<sub>2</sub> and becomes H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, so it is the base.

q: Which species is amphoteric, able to act as either an acid or a base?
h: An amphoteric species needs an H to give and room to take one.
w: HCO3− can donate or accept a proton.
x: Carbonate has no H to donate, so it can act only as a base.
Chloride has no H to donate and is too weak a base to take one; it is a spectator ion.
Na<sup>+</sup> neither donates nor accepts protons; it is a spectator ion.

q: Which acid is a strong acid?
h: Strong acids: HCl, HBr, HI, HNO<sub>3</sub>, HClO<sub>4</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.
w: HI is on the strong-acid list; the others are weak.
x: Nitrous acid (HNO<sub>2</sub>) is not nitric acid (HNO<sub>3</sub>); it is not on the strong list, so it is weak.
Lactic acid is not on the strong list, so it is weak.
Carbonic acid is weak; it is the acid partner of the blood buffer.

q: Nitrous acid, HNO<sub>2</sub>, is a weak acid. Which equation correctly shows it ionizing in water?
h: Weak acid: double arrow, and the acid gives its H<sup>+</sup> to water.
w: HNO2(aq) + H2O(l) ⇄ H3O+(aq) + NO2−(aq) (double arrow for a weak acid).
x: A single arrow means complete ionization, which is only for strong acids.
This has the acid accepting a proton from water; an acid donates its proton.
This shows a single arrow (complete ionization) and leaves out the water that takes the proton; a weak acid needs a double arrow.

q: Acetic acid, HC<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, is dissolved in water. Which description fits the solution (water molecules not counted)?
c: Mostly intact HC<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>O<sub>2</sub> molecules, with a few H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> and C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>O<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> ions
Only H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> and C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>O<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> ions, with no intact molecules
Only intact HC<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>O<sub>2</sub> molecules, with no ions at all
Mostly H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> ions and intact molecules, but no acetate ions
h: Weak acids ionize only slightly.
w: Weak acid: mostly intact molecules, a few ions.
x: All ions and no molecules describes a strong acid; acetic acid is weak.
A weak acid does ionize a little, which is why vinegar conducts weakly.
Each molecule that ionizes makes one H3O+ and one acetate ion.

q: Solution A is 0.0020 M HNO<sub>3</sub>; solution B is 3.0 M HC<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>O<sub>2</sub>. Which statement is true?
c: A is a dilute solution of a strong acid; B is a concentrated solution of a weak acid.
A is a weak acid because it is dilute; B is a strong acid because it is concentrated.
Both are strong acids, because both ionize completely.
Both are weak acids, because both contain intact acid molecules.
h: Strong or weak depends on which acid it is, not on how much is dissolved.
w: HNO3 is strong (but dilute here); acetic acid is weak (but concentrated here): A dilute strong acid, B concentrated weak acid.
x: This mixes up strength with concentration. Dilute HNO<sub>3</sub> is still fully ionized.
Acetic acid is weak at any concentration; most of its molecules stay intact.
HNO<sub>3</sub> is strong: even dilute, it has essentially no intact molecules.

q: Isopropyl alcohol (rubbing alcohol), C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>OH, contains an OH group. How is it classified?
c: Neither an acid nor a base
h: Is the OH a hydroxide ion or a covalent group?
w: An alcohol's OH is not OH−: neither an acid nor a base.
x: Strong bases are ionic metal hydroxides that release OH<sup>−</sup>; an alcohol does not.
Weak bases are ammonia, amines, carbonates, and bicarbonates; an alcohol is none of these.
Alcohols do not have an acidic H written first or a –COOH group.

q: Hydroiodic acid neutralizes barium hydroxide. What salt forms?
h: Salt = base's cation + acid's anion, with balanced charges.
