w: 2 HI(aq) + Ba(OH)2(aq) → BaI2(aq) + 2 H2O(l): BaI2.
x: BaI leaves the charges unbalanced: Ba<sup>2+</sup> needs two I<sup>−</sup>.
This swaps the subscripts the wrong way; Ba<sup>2+</sup> needs two iodide ions, not two barium ions.
The salt is the base's cation with the acid's anion; the H<sup>+</sup> ends up in water.

q: A sample of tomato juice has [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] = 7.9 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M at 25 °C. What is [OH<sup>−</sup>]?
h: Divide K<sub>w</sub> by the concentration you know.
w: [OH−] = 1.0 × 10−14 / 7.9 × 10−5 = 1.3 × 10−10 M.
x: This multiplies by K<sub>w</sub>; the product [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>][OH<sup>−</sup>] equals K<sub>w</sub>, so divide.
This divides the wrong way (concentration / K<sub>w</sub>), giving an impossible value.
1.0 × 10<sup>−7</sup> M is [OH<sup>−</sup>] in pure water; an acidic juice has less.

q: Use the table (all at 25 °C). Which solution is the most acidic?
h: Convert every [OH<sup>−</sup>] to [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] with K<sub>w</sub>, then compare.
w: A 4.1 × 10−5, B 1.3 × 10−12, C 9.0 × 10−9, D 3.0 × 10−3 M [H3O+]: Solution D.
x: A has [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] = 4.1 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M, acidic but less than D's 3.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> M.
B has a large [OH<sup>−</sup>], so it is basic.
C has [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] below 10<sup>−7</sup> M, so it is basic.

q: What is [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] in 0.0012 M Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> at 25 °C?
h: Double first, then divide K<sub>w</sub> by [OH<sup>−</sup>].
w: [OH−] = 0.0024 M; [H3O+] = 1.0 × 10−14 / 0.0024 = 4.2 × 10−12 M.
x: This forgets to double [OH<sup>−</sup>]: Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> gives two hydroxides.
0.0024 M is [OH<sup>−</sup>]; the question asks for [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>].
This multiplies by K<sub>w</sub>; divide K<sub>w</sub> by [OH<sup>−</sup>].

q: A few drops of acid are added to pure water at 25 °C, and [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] rises. What happens to [OH<sup>−</sup>]?
c: It drops to zero, because an acidic solution has no OH<sup>−</sup>.
h: The product of the two concentrations is fixed at 25 °C.
w: At 25 °C, [H3O+][OH−] = Kw = 1.0 × 10−14 in every water solution. When [H3O+] rises, [OH−] must fall to keep the product constant. It never drops all the way to zero, because water always ionizes a little.
x: If both rose, their product would grow larger than K<sub>w</sub>.
[OH<sup>−</sup>] is 1.0 × 10<sup>−7</sup> M only when the solution is neutral.
Every water solution contains both ions; [OH<sup>−</sup>] gets small but never zero.

q: The relationship K<sub>w</sub> = [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>][OH<sup>−</sup>] = 1.0 × 10<sup>−14</sup> applies to which solutions at 25 °C?
c: Every water solution: acidic, basic, or neutral
Only solutions of strong acids and bases
h: What stays the same when an acid is added to water?
w: Kw applies to every water solution at 25 °C.
x: It is found from pure water, but it stays true when acids or bases are added.
Acidic and basic solutions obey it too; only the balance between the two ions changes.
Weak acids and bases, salts, and blood obey it as well.

q: What is the pH of 0.0033 M Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub> at 25 °C?
h: Double [OH<sup>−</sup>] for Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub>, then pOH, then pH.
x: This forgets to double [OH<sup>−</sup>]: each Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub> releases two hydroxide ions.
This is the pOH; subtract it from 14.00.
This has only one decimal place; the concentration has 2 significant figures.

q: A hand soap solution has pH 9.62 at 25 °C. What is its [OH<sup>−</sup>]?
h: Find the pOH first, then [OH<sup>−</sup>] = 10<sup>−pOH</sup>.
w: pOH = 4.38; [OH−] = 10−4.38 = 4.2 × 10−5 M.
x: 10<sup>−9.62</sup> is [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>], not [OH<sup>−</sup>].
4.38 is the pOH; it is not a concentration. Take 10<sup>−pOH</sup>.
This leaves out the minus sign: 10<sup>4.38</sup> instead of 10<sup>−4.38</sup>.

q: Four solutions have pH 8.3, 2.5, 6.5, and 11.5. Which list puts them in order of increasing acidity (least acidic first)?
h: Lower pH = more acidic.
w: Least acidic (highest pH) to most acidic: 11.5, 8.3, 6.5, 2.5.
x: This is decreasing acidity (most acidic first); lower pH means more acidic.
This order does not follow the pH values at all; sort by pH, highest first.
This is not sorted; least acidic means the highest pH.

q: A patient's arterial blood gas shows pH 7.52. How is this described?
c: Neutral, because it is close to 7
h: Compare with the normal arterial range, 7.35–7.45.
w: Normal arterial blood pH is 7.35–7.45. Because 7.52 is above 7.45, this is alkalosis. Calling it neutral is a trap: blood is judged against its own normal range, not against pH 7.00.
x: Acidosis is a pH below 7.35.
7.52 is outside the normal range, which ends at 7.45.
Blood is judged against its own normal range, 7.35–7.45, not against 7.00.

q: What is a buffer?
c: A solution that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added
A solution whose pH is exactly 7.00
A mixture of a strong acid and a strong base
A solution whose pH never changes, no matter how much acid is added
h: Think of what blood does when acid enters it.
w: A buffer resists pH change when small amounts of acid or base are added.
x: Buffers can hold a pH far from 7; an acetate buffer is acidic.
A strong acid and a strong base simply neutralize each other; neither part remains to absorb more.
A buffer has a limited capacity; add too much acid and the pH falls sharply.

q: Which mixture is not a buffer?
h: Look for a strong acid or base: it cannot be part of a buffer.
w: HI is on the strong-acid list: HI and NaI is not a buffer.
x: HF is weak and F<sup>−</sup> is its conjugate base: a buffer.
NH<sub>3</sub> is a weak base and NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> is its conjugate acid: a buffer.
H<sub>2</sub>PO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> and HPO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> differ by one H<sup>+</sup>, and neither is strong: a buffer.

q: A buffer contains HF and F<sup>−</sup>. Which equation shows it neutralizing a small amount of added OH<sup>−</sup>?
h: Added base is neutralized by the acid partner.
w: HF(aq) + OH−(aq) → F−(aq) + H2O(l).
x: This is how the buffer handles added acid.
A buffer has very little H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> on hand; the HF partner is what absorbs OH<sup>−</sup>.
This is HF ionizing in water; it does not use up the added OH<sup>−</sup>.

q: The body can adjust both partners of the bicarbonate buffer. Which organ controls the blood's HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> level, and how fast?
c: The kidneys, over hours to days
h: Lungs handle CO<sub>2</sub>; which organ handles bicarbonate?
w: The kidneys, over hours to days (the lungs adjust CO2 in minutes).
x: The lungs control CO<sub>2</sub> (and so H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>) within minutes; bicarbonate is the kidneys' job.
The organ is right, but the kidneys act slowly, over hours to days.
Stomach acid does not set blood bicarbonate; the kidneys do.

q: A buffer is made with 0.10 mol of a weak acid, HA, and 0.10 mol of its conjugate base, A<sup>−</sup>. Then 0.20 mol of HCl is added. What happens?
c: The A<sup>−</sup> is used up after 0.10 mol of HCl, and the extra acid makes the pH drop sharply.
The pH stays nearly constant, because buffers absorb any amount of acid.
The HA neutralizes the added HCl, so the pH rises.
The pH stays nearly constant, because HCl is a weak acid in a buffer.
h: Compare the moles of HCl with the moles of A<sup>−</sup>.
w: 0.20 mol HCl > 0.10 mol A−: the capacity is exceeded, and the pH drops sharply.
x: A buffer has a limited capacity, set by how much of each partner it contains.
HA is the acid partner; it reacts with added base, not added acid.
HCl is a strong acid in any solution.

q: According to collision theory, which two things must be true of a collision for it to form products?
c: The particles must hit with the right orientation and with at least the activation energy.
The particles must hit with the right orientation; any amount of energy is enough.
The particles must hit with at least the activation energy; the direction they hit from does not matter.
The particles only need to collide; every collision forms products.
h: Think of the two conditions that make a collision effective.
w: An effective collision has the right orientation and at least Ea.
x: A gentle collision with the right orientation still fails if it does not reach the activation energy.
Even a hard collision fails if the wrong parts of the molecules touch, because the right bonds cannot break and form.
Most collisions do not form products; only effective collisions do.

q: On a reaction's energy diagram, the reactants are at 88 kJ, the products are at 23 kJ, and the peak of the hill is at 142 kJ. What is ΔH, and is the reaction exothermic or endothermic?
h: ΔH = energy of the products − energy of the reactants.
w: ΔH = 23 kJ − 88 kJ = −65 kJ, exothermic.
x: This is reactants − products. ΔH is products − reactants, which is negative here.
This is the activation energy (142 − 88), the height of the hill, not ΔH.
This measures from the peak of the hill down to the products; ΔH compares only the start and the end.

q: Full-strength household bleach removes a coffee stain from a white shirt much faster than bleach diluted with water. Why?
c: More hypochlorite ions per milliliter means more frequent collisions with the stain.
The added water acts as a catalyst that slows the reaction down.
Diluting the bleach raises the activation energy of the reaction.
Full-strength bleach is hotter, so its ions move faster than in diluted bleach.
h: A higher concentration of a reactant: what happens to the number of collisions?
w: Higher concentration → more collisions per second → faster stain removal.
x: Water is not a catalyst here, and a catalyst speeds a reaction up rather than slowing it.
Concentration changes the number of collisions, not the height of the energy hill.
Both bleaches are at room temperature, so heat is not the difference.

q: The table shows the relative rate of a reaction catalyzed by a human enzyme at several temperatures. Why does the rate fall above 37 °C?
c: The enzyme begins to change shape (denature), so it catalyzes the reaction less well.
Higher temperatures always make reactions slower.
Above 37 °C the molecules collide less often.
The activation energy of every reaction rises above 37 °C.
h: Enzymes are proteins with a working shape.
w: The rate peaks at 37 °C (1.00), then falls: the enzyme denatures.
x: Below 37 °C the rate rises with temperature, as for most reactions. The drop above 37 °C comes from the enzyme itself.
Molecules move faster and collide more often as the temperature rises; collisions are not the problem.
E<sub>a</sub> does not jump at 37 °C; the enzyme loses its working shape, so the catalyzed path is lost.

q: At the same temperature, reaction A has E<sub>a</sub> = 24 kJ and reaction B has E<sub>a</sub> = 96 kJ. Which statement is correct?
c: Reaction A is faster, because a larger fraction of its collisions have at least its activation energy.
Reaction B is faster, because a higher activation energy releases more energy.
They have the same rate, because the temperature is the same.
Reaction B is faster, because its molecules have more energy.
h: Lower hill or higher hill: which one do more collisions get over?
w: Lower Ea (24 kJ) → reaction A is faster.
x: E<sub>a</sub> is the energy needed to start the reaction, not the energy released; a higher hill makes a reaction slower.
At the same temperature, the reaction with the lower hill has more effective collisions, so it is faster.
At the same temperature the molecules have the same average energy; B needs more of it to react.

q: A blood sample is cooled from 37 °C to 27 °C. Using the rule of thumb that many reaction rates about double for every 10 °C rise, about how fast do the sample's enzyme-catalyzed reactions run at 27 °C compared with 37 °C?
h: Is the sample warmer or cooler, and by how many 10 °C steps?
w: One 10 °C step cooler → about half as fast.
x: Cooling slows reactions down; twice as fast would be for 10 °C warmer.
A 10 °C change has a large effect on most reaction rates.
The rule of thumb is a factor of about 2 for each 10 °C, not a factor of 10.

q: The graph shows [A] and [B] over time for the reaction A ⇄ B in a sealed flask that started with only A. When is equilibrium first reached?
c: At about 50 s, when both curves become flat
At about 22 s, where the two curves cross
At 0 s, when the reaction starts
At 100 s, when the reactions stop
h: Look for the time after which neither line changes.
w: Both lines are flat from about 50 s on: equilibrium at about 50 s.
x: The crossing point is where [A] = [B]. Both concentrations are still changing there, and equal concentrations are not the sign of equilibrium.
At 0 s there is no B yet, so the reverse reaction has not started and the forward rate is much faster.
The lines are flat well before 100 s, and the reactions never stop; they continue at equal rates.

q:
A sealed flask starts with only H2 and Br2, which react:
H2(g) + Br2(g) ⇄ 2 HBr(g)
What happens to the forward and reverse rates as the system approaches equilibrium?
c: The forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises until they are equal.
The forward rate rises and the reverse rate falls until they are equal.
Both rates fall until they reach zero.
Both rates stay the same the whole time.
h: At the start there is lots of reactant and no product.
w: Forward falls, reverse rises, until they are equal.
x: This has it backward: the forward rate is highest at the start, when the most reactant is present.
The rates become equal, not zero; both reactions keep running.
The forward rate starts high and the reverse rate starts at zero, so they must change to become equal.

q:
A sealed flask at a fixed temperature starts with only COCl2 gas. What happens?
CO(g) + Cl2(g) ⇄ COCl2(g)
c: Some COCl<sub>2</sub> breaks down until the forward and reverse rates are equal, giving a mixture of all three gases.
Nothing happens, because equilibrium can be reached only by starting from the reactants.
All of the COCl<sub>2</sub> breaks down into CO and Cl<sub>2</sub>.
It reaches a mixture that has a different K than a mixture made from CO and Cl<sub>2</sub>.
h: Can equilibrium be reached from the product side?
w: Partial breakdown to an equilibrium mixture of all three gases, with the same K.
x: Equilibrium can be approached from the product side as well.
As soon as CO and Cl<sub>2</sub> form, they react to re-form COCl<sub>2</sub>, so the breakdown is not complete.
At the same temperature, the mixture obeys the same K no matter which side it started from.

q:
Why does an open glass of soda go flat instead of reaching an equilibrium between dissolved and gaseous CO2?
CO2(aq) ⇄ CO2(g)
c: The CO<sub>2</sub> gas escapes the open glass, and equilibrium needs a closed system.
Gases cannot take part in an equilibrium with a dissolved substance.
The forward and reverse rates become equal, so the CO<sub>2</sub> leaves.
Dissolving CO<sub>2</sub> in water is not a reversible process at all.
h: What does an equilibrium need that an open glass does not have?
w: The gas escapes: equilibrium needs a closed system.
x: Gases take part in many equilibria, for example in a sealed soda bottle.
Equal rates would mean no net loss of CO₂. The soda goes flat because the rates are not equal.
CO₂ dissolves and leaves the liquid in both directions. In a sealed bottle the two processes balance.

q:
A chemist swaps a tiny fraction of the CO in an equilibrium mixture for CO made with carbon-14, keeping [CO] the same.
CO(g) + Cl2(g) ⇄ COCl2(g)
Later, carbon-14 shows up in COCl2 molecules, but no concentration ever changes. What does this show?
c: Both reactions are still running at equal rates, so labeled carbon atoms move into COCl<sub>2</sub> and back out.
The reaction had stopped, and adding the labeled CO restarted it in the forward direction only.
The forward rate is faster than the reverse rate at equilibrium.
Carbon-14 is a catalyst that makes new COCl<sub>2</sub>.
h: How can labeled atoms end up in the product if nothing changes?
w: The label spreads with no net change: both reactions run at equal rates.
x: Nothing restarted; [CO] did not change, and the label spreads only because both reactions were already running.
If the forward rate were faster, [COCl<sub>2</sub>] would rise; it stays constant.
Carbon-14 is just a labeled carbon atom; it reacts like ordinary carbon and is not a catalyst.

q: At equilibrium, a reaction mixture contains far more product than reactant. Which statement is true?
c: The forward and reverse rates are equal; the equilibrium mixture of this reaction simply favors products.
The forward rate is faster than the reverse rate, which is why there is more product.
The reverse reaction has stopped, so product builds up.
The system will not be at equilibrium until the amounts become equal.
h: Do unequal amounts mean unequal rates?
w: Equal rates; this reaction just favors products.
x: A faster forward rate would keep making product, so the concentrations would not be constant.
Both reactions run at equilibrium; neither one stops.
Equilibrium means constant amounts, not equal amounts.

q:
Write the equilibrium constant expression for
2 H2(g) + O2(g) ⇄ 2 H2O(l)
h: Which species are left out? What is left on top when every product is a liquid?
w: Pure liquids such as H2O(l) are left out of K, so no product term remains on top. Each reactant is raised to the power of its coefficient: K = 1 / ([H2]2[O2]). Writing [H2O]2 on top is the main trap, because a pure liquid has no changing concentration.
x: H<sub>2</sub>O(l) is a pure liquid, so it is left out of K.
The reactants belong in the denominator; with no product term left, the expression is 1 over the reactants.
The coefficient 2 on H<sub>2</sub> must become an exponent of 2.

q: Which reaction has the equilibrium constant expression K = [CO<sub>2</sub>]?
h: For each reaction, cross out (s) and (l), then write products over reactants.
w: Only the CO2 is not a solid, and it is a product: MgCO3(s) ⇄ MgO(s) + CO2(g).
x: Here K = [CO]<sup>2</sup> / [CO<sub>2</sub>]; carbon is a solid, but CO is a gas product.
Here K = [H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>] / [CO<sub>2</sub>]; only the liquid water is left out.
Here CO<sub>2</sub> is a reactant, so K = 1 / [CO<sub>2</sub>].

q:
Nitrosyl chloride breaks down:
2 NOCl(g) ⇄ 2 NO(g) + Cl2(g)
At equilibrium, [NOCl] = 0.344 M, [NO] = 0.0613 M, and [Cl2] = 0.0307 M. Calculate K.
h: Write K first: products over reactants, coefficients as exponents.
w: K = (0.0613)2(0.0307) / (0.344)2 = 9.75 × 10−4. K < 1, so reactants are favored.
x: This is reactants over products, the inverse of K.
This leaves out the exponents; [NO] and [NOCl] must each be squared.
This adds the product concentrations; concentrations in K are multiplied, and each is raised to its coefficient.

q:
Hot charcoal reacts with carbon dioxide in a closed vessel:
C(s) + CO2(g) ⇄ 2 CO(g)
At equilibrium, [CO2] = 0.0371 M and [CO] = 0.115 M. Calculate K.
h: Leave out the solid, then square the CO term.
w: C(s) is a pure solid, so it is left out: K = [CO]2 / [CO2]. K = (0.115)2 / 0.0371 = 0.356. Forgetting to square [CO] gives 3.10, and flipping the fraction gives 2.81.
x: This is reactants over products, the inverse of K.
This forgets to square [CO]; its coefficient is 2.
This multiplies [CO] by 2; the coefficient becomes an exponent, not a multiplier.

q:
At a certain temperature, K = 0.0384 for
2 NO2(g) ⇄ 2 NO(g) + O2(g)
What is K for the reverse reaction,
2 NO(g) + O2(g) ⇄ 2 NO2(g)
at the same temperature?
h: Products and reactants trade places. What does that do to the fraction?
w: Reversing a reaction swaps products and reactants, so the new K is the reciprocal of the old one: Kreverse = 1 / 0.0384 = 26.0. K stays the same only if the reaction is unchanged, it is never negative, and 1 − K (0.962) has no meaning here.
x: Reversing the reaction flips products and reactants, so K becomes 1/K; it does not stay the same.
K is never negative. (Reversing a reaction flips the sign of ΔH, not of K.)
The reverse K is the reciprocal (1 divided by K), not 1 minus K.

q:
The burning of glucose,
C6H12O6(s) + 6 O2(g) ⇄ 6 CO2(g) + 6 H2O(l)
has an enormous K at room temperature, yet sugar sits in a bowl in air for years without burning. How can both be true?
c: K tells how far a reaction goes, not how fast; the activation energy is high, so at room temperature the reaction is extremely slow.
A large K means a fast reaction, so the sugar must be burning without anyone noticing.
Air does not contain enough oxygen for the reaction to start.
A large K means the mixture is already at equilibrium, so nothing can happen.
h: Does K measure how far or how fast?
w: Large K = how far, not how fast; a high Ea keeps the reaction slow.
x: A large K is not a fast rate; if the sugar were burning, the bowl would be empty.
Air is about 21% oxygen, plenty for burning; the barrier is the activation energy.
Sugar and oxygen are far from equilibrium; they would form CO<sub>2</sub> and water if the reaction could get going.

q:
In a hydrogen plant, CO2 is removed from this equilibrium mixture by absorbing it into a solution:
CO(g) + H2O(g) ⇄ CO2(g) + H2(g)
Which way does the equilibrium shift?
c: Shifts right, toward the removed CO<sub>2</sub>
Shifts left, away from the removed CO<sub>2</sub>
No shift, because CO<sub>2</sub> is a product
h: Take → toward.
w: CO2 is removed: shifts right, toward it, making more H2.
x: Removing a substance pulls the system toward it, to replace some of what was taken.
Changing the amount of a product shifts an equilibrium just as changing a reactant does.
The shift is to the right, and K does not change unless the temperature changes.

q:
Some NO2 is added to this mixture at equilibrium:
2 NO(g) + O2(g) ⇄ 2 NO2(g)
Once the new equilibrium is reached, what has happened to [O2]?
h: First find the direction of the shift, then follow it to O<sub>2</sub>.
w: Add → away: shift left, so [O2] increases.
x: This would happen after a shift to the right; adding a product shifts the system left.
The shift to the left changes every concentration, including [O<sub>2</sub>].
The concentration change is right, but K changes only with temperature.

q:
More powdered carbon is added to this mixture at equilibrium:
C(s) + CO2(g) ⇄ 2 CO(g)
Which way does the equilibrium shift?
c: No shift, because a pure solid does not appear in K
Shifts right, away from the added carbon
Shifts left, toward the added carbon
h: Is C(s) part of the K expression?
w: A pure solid has no concentration term in K = [CO]2 / [CO2], so adding more C(s) changes neither Q nor K, and there is no shift. The rule “add a substance, shift away from it” applies only to gases and dissolved species.
x: Add → away applies to gases and dissolved species; a pure solid has no concentration term in K.
Adding a substance never shifts the system toward it, and a solid causes no shift at all.
Adding a solid neither shifts the system nor changes K.

q:
The volume of the container is decreased for this mixture at equilibrium:
H2(g) + Br2(g) ⇄ 2 HBr(g)
Which way does the equilibrium shift?
c: No shift, because both sides have 2 moles of gas
Shifts left, toward H<sub>2</sub> and Br<sub>2</sub>
h: Count moles of gas on each side.
w: Decreasing the volume shifts an equilibrium toward the side with fewer moles of gas. Here both sides have 2 mol of gas (1 + 1 on the left, 2 on the right), so there is no shift. A shift toward HBr would need fewer gas moles on the right, and a volume change never changes K.
x: A shift happens only when one side has fewer moles of gas; here both sides have 2.
Both sides have the same number of gas moles, so there is no side with fewer moles to shift toward.
There is no shift, and a volume change never changes K.

q:
During a panic attack, a patient breathes much faster than her body needs and blows off CO2. What happens to this equilibrium in her blood?
CO2(aq) + H2O(l) ⇄ H2CO3(aq) ⇄ H+(aq) + HCO3−(aq)
c: Shifts left, [H<sup>+</sup>] decreases, and blood pH rises
Shifts right, [H<sup>+</sup>] increases, and blood pH falls
Shifts left, [H<sup>+</sup>] decreases, and blood pH falls
No shift, because the kidneys keep [H<sup>+</sup>] fixed
h: Fast breathing removes CO<sub>2</sub>. Which way does take → toward point?
w: Remove CO2 → shifts left, less H+, pH rises.
x: This happens when CO<sub>2</sub> builds up, as in hypoventilation; fast breathing removes CO<sub>2</sub>.
Less H<sup>+</sup> means a higher pH, not a lower one.
The kidneys respond only slowly, over hours to days; the fast change comes from the shift.

q:
Which change shifts this enamel equilibrium toward demineralization (dissolving)?
Ca5(PO4)3OH(s) ⇄ 5 Ca2+(aq) + 3 PO43−(aq) + OH−(aq)
c: Acid from plaque bacteria removing OH<sup>−</sup> ions
A remineralizing paste adding Ca<sup>2+</sup> and phosphate ions
h: Dissolving is the forward direction. Which change pulls the system to the right?
w: Removing a product shifts right: acid removing OH−.
x: Adding Ca<sup>2+</sup>, a product, shifts the system left, toward remineralization.
Adding phosphate, a product, shifts the system left, toward remineralization.
Adding products shifts the system left, which rebuilds enamel.

q:
Ammonia plants run the exothermic Haber process,
N2(g) + 3 H2(g) ⇄ 2 NH3(g)
at about 400–450 °C, even though a lower temperature would give more NH3 at equilibrium. Why?
c: At a low temperature the reaction is far too slow, so a higher temperature is used to make NH<sub>3</sub> at a useful rate
A low temperature would lower K and give less NH<sub>3</sub>
A high temperature shifts the equilibrium toward NH<sub>3</sub>
A high temperature lets the iron catalyst shift the equilibrium toward NH<sub>3</sub>
h: Low temperature helps the yield. What does it do to the rate?
w: Equilibrium favors low T, but the rate would be far too slow; plants compromise.
x: For an exothermic reaction, lowering the temperature raises K and favors NH<sub>3</sub>.
Heat is a product of this reaction, so raising the temperature shifts it left, away from NH<sub>3</sub>.
A catalyst never shifts an equilibrium; it helps the plant reach equilibrium faster.

q: Strontium-90 is a radioisotope found in nuclear fallout. How many protons and neutrons are in one strontium-90 nucleus?
h: Z comes from the periodic table; neutrons = A − Z.
w: 9038Sr: Z = 38 protons; 90 − 38 = 52 neutrons.
x: This swaps the two counts. The atomic number (38, from the periodic table) is the number of protons.
90 is the mass number, protons + neutrons together; subtract the 38 protons to get the neutrons.
The mass number 90 counts protons and neutrons together; the protons are the atomic number, 38.

q: A radiation therapy plan prescribes 2 Gy to a tumor in each session. What does a dose in grays describe?
c: The energy absorbed per kilogram of tumor tissue (1 Gy = 1 J/kg)
How many nuclei in the source decay each second
The absorbed dose adjusted for how harmful each kind of radiation is
How long each treatment session lasts
h: The gray replaced the older unit, the rad.
w: Absorbed dose: 1 Gy = 1 J of energy per kg of tissue.
x: Decays per second is the activity of a source, in becquerels or curies.
That is the equivalent (biological) dose, measured in sieverts or rem.
A gray is an amount of absorbed energy per mass, not a time.

q: An indium-111 dose has an activity of 18.0 mCi. What is its activity in becquerels? (1 Ci = 3.7 × 10<sup>10</sup> Bq, exact)
h: mCi → Ci (divide by 1000), then Ci → Bq.
w: 18.0 mCi × (1 Ci / 1000 mCi) × (3.7 × 1010 Bq / 1 Ci) = 6.66 × 108 Bq.
x: This skips the mCi → Ci step; 1 Ci = 1000 mCi, so 18.0 mCi is only 0.0180 Ci.
This divides by 3.7 × 10<sup>10</sup>. Each curie is a huge number of becquerels, so multiply.
This multiplies by 1000 to go from mCi to Ci; a curie is larger than a millicurie, so divide by 1000.

q: How does a Geiger counter detect radiation?
c: Radiation ionizes the gas in a sealed tube, and each burst of ions lets a pulse of current flow, counted as a click.
Radiation makes a crystal give off flashes of light, which a light detector counts.
Radiation darkens a strip of photographic film over a month of use.
The counter measures the heat given off by the radioactive sample.
h: Radiation is called ionizing for a reason.
w: A Geiger counter counts the current pulses made when radiation ionizes the gas in its tube.
x: That is a scintillation counter, the detector inside a gamma camera.
That is a film badge, which records a worker's total dose over time.
The heat from a medical source is far too small to measure; detectors count ions or light.

q: Sodium-22 is used as a small source to check PET scanners. Identify the missing particle: <sup>22</sup><sub>11</sub>Na → <sup>22</sup><sub>10</sub>Ne + ?
h: Subtract: what A and Z must the particle have?
w: A: 22 = 22 + 0. Z: 11 = 10 + 1. The particle is a positron, 0+1e.
x: A beta particle (Z = −1) would make the new atomic number one higher (12, magnesium), not lower.
An alpha particle would lower A by 4; here A does not change.
A gamma ray changes neither A nor Z, but here Z drops from 11 to 10.

q: Iodine-123, used for thyroid imaging, decays by electron capture. What is the product? <sup>123</sup><sub>53</sub>I + <sup>0</sup><sub>−1</sub>e → ?
h: In electron capture the electron is a reactant: add it on the left.
w: A: 123 + 0 = 123. Z: 53 − 1 = 52 (tellurium): 12352Te.
x: This raises Z, as if a beta particle were given off. In electron capture the electron is taken in, so Z drops by 1.
The electron has a mass number of 0, so A stays 123.
A proton becomes a neutron, so Z changes and the element changes.

q: Iodine-123 is made in a cyclotron by hitting tellurium-124 with protons; two neutrons come out. Complete the equation: <sup>124</sup><sub>52</sub>Te + <sup>1</sup><sub>1</sub>H → ? + 2 <sup>1</sup><sub>0</sub>n
h: Total the left side, then subtract 2 × the neutron.
x: This counts only one neutron; the coefficient 2 means 2 mass units leave.
This forgets the neutrons on the right; they carry away 2 mass units.
This forgets the proton's charge: Z on the left is 52 + 1 = 53.

q: Chlorine-36 helps date very old groundwater. What kind of decay is this? <sup>36</sup><sub>17</sub>Cl → <sup>36</sup><sub>18</sub>Ar + <sup>0</sup><sub>−1</sub>e
h: Look at which particle is a product and whether Z goes up or down.
w: The product 0−1e and Z + 1 with A unchanged: beta decay.
x: Positron emission gives off <sup>0</sup><sub>+1</sub>e and lowers Z by 1; here Z rises.
Alpha decay gives off <sup>4</sup><sub>2</sub>He and lowers A by 4; here A does not change.
In electron capture the electron is on the left as a reactant and Z drops by 1.

q: Radium-224 forms when a parent nucleus gives off an alpha particle. What is the parent? ? → <sup>224</sup><sub>88</sub>Ra + <sup>4</sup><sub>2</sub>He
h: The parent is on the left: add the right-side numbers.
x: This subtracts the alpha particle instead of adding it; the parent is heavier than its daughter.
This adds only 1 to Z; the alpha particle carries 2 protons, so Z = 90.
This keeps Z = 88; the parent must have 2 more protons than radium.

q: Outside the body, which kind of radiation is the biggest concern for a nuclear medicine technologist, and why?
c: Gamma rays, because they pass through the body and reach internal organs
Alpha particles, because they are the most ionizing
Beta particles, because they are the most penetrating
Alpha particles, because they are the most penetrating
h: From outside, the radiation must first get through the skin.
w: Outside the body: gamma rays, the most penetrating.
x: Alpha particles are the most ionizing, but from outside they cannot get through the dead outer layer of skin. (Inside the body they are the most damaging.)
Beta particles are only medium in penetrating power; a lab coat and gloves stop most of them.
Alpha particles are the least penetrating; paper or skin stops them.

q: The half-life of cobalt-60 is known very precisely (5.27 years). Why can no one predict the moment one particular cobalt-60 nucleus will decay?
c: Each nucleus decays at a random moment; the half-life describes what a very large number of nuclei do.
Each nucleus decays exactly 5.27 years after it forms, but no one knows when it formed.
A single nucleus decays faster than a large sample does.
The half-life changes with the temperature of the source.
h: Is decay a timer or a chance event?
w: Decay is random for each nucleus; half-life is a property of large numbers of nuclei.
x: Nuclei do not carry a timer; half of them decay in the first half-life and half of the rest in the next.
Half-life does not depend on the amount; one nucleus and a large sample follow the same odds.
Temperature does not change half-life.

q: Gallium-67 (half-life 3.26 days) is used to image infections. A patient's dose is measured 9.78 days after it was made, and 0.650 mCi remains. What was the activity when it was made?
h: Working backward, double once per half-life.
w: 9.78 days ÷ 3.26 days = 3 half-lives. Working backward, double the activity once per half-life: 0.650 mCi × 23 = 5.20 mCi. Multiplying by 3 instead of 23 = 8 gives 1.95 mCi, the most common trap.
x: This doubles only twice; 9.78 days is 3 half-lives.
This doubles four times; n = 9.78 ÷ 3.26 = 3.
This multiplies by n = 3. Working backward doubles 3 times, a factor of 8.

q: Why must a PET center use fluorine-18 FDG within a few hours of making it?
c: Its half-life is only 110 min, so most of it decays within a few hours.
Its activity rises over time, so a later dose would be too strong.
Its half-life gets shorter as the sample gets older.
It loses its fluorine atoms to the air, even though its nuclei do not decay.
h: Look up fluorine-18 in the half-life table.
w: Fluorine-18's 110 min half-life is short.
x: Activity only falls as the nuclei decay.
Half-life is constant for each isotope.
The problem is nuclear decay, not loss of atoms.

q: How is carbon-14 made in the upper atmosphere?
c: Neutrons from cosmic rays hit nitrogen-14 nuclei: <sup>14</sup><sub>7</sub>N + <sup>1</sup><sub>0</sub>n → <sup>14</sup><sub>6</sub>C + <sup>1</sup><sub>1</sub>H
Carbon-12 atoms absorb two neutrons from sunlight: <sup>12</sup><sub>6</sub>C + 2 <sup>1</sup><sub>0</sub>n → <sup>14</sup><sub>6</sub>C
Carbon-14 is left over from when Earth formed and has not decayed yet
h: Most of the atmosphere is nitrogen.
w: 147N + 10n → 146C + 11H, driven by cosmic-ray neutrons.
x: This equation balances, but it is not how carbon-14 forms; carbon-14 comes from the nitrogen in the air.
With a half-life of 5730 years, any carbon-14 from Earth's formation (4.5 billion years ago) decayed long ago; it is constantly remade.
Plants take in carbon-14 that is already in the CO<sub>2</sub> of the air; they do not make it.

q: An animal dies. What happens to the ratio of carbon-14 to carbon-12 in its bones over the next several thousand years?
c: It decreases, because carbon-14 decays and is no longer replaced
It increases, because carbon-14 builds up after death
It stays the same, because the bones keep exchanging carbon with the air
It drops to zero right away, because carbon-14 decays at death
h: After death, is carbon-14 still replaced?
w: Carbon-14 decays and is not replaced: the ratio decreases.
x: Nothing adds carbon-14 to a dead organism; it only decays away.
Exchange stops at death: no more eating or photosynthesis.
It halves only every 5730 years; it does not vanish at once.

q: Carbon from living plants gives 13.6 decays per minute per gram of carbon. Charcoal from an ancient campfire gives 3.40 decays per minute per gram. Estimate the charcoal's age. (carbon-14 half-life 5730 years)
h: Turn the activities into a number of halvings, n.
w: n = 2: age = 2 × 5730 = 1.15 × 104 years.
x: This uses the 4 from the fraction 1/4 as the number of half-lives. 1/4 = (1/2)<sup>2</sup>, so n = 2.
This multiplies the fraction (1/4) by 5730. First find n, then multiply n × 5730 years.
This counts the three activities in the chain; count the two halvings.

q: A cave painting has black lines drawn with charcoal and red areas painted with red ochre, a mineral (iron oxide). Which part can be dated with carbon-14?
c: Only the charcoal lines, because charcoal is once-living wood
Only the red ochre, because iron oxide holds carbon-14 from the air
Both, because everything in a cave has the same carbon-14 ratio
Neither, because pigments cannot contain carbon
h: Radiocarbon dating needs something that was once alive.
w: Only once-living material can be dated: the charcoal.
x: Iron oxide contains no carbon at all, and it was never alive.
Only once-living material carries a carbon-14 clock; minerals do not.
Charcoal is almost pure carbon; that is why it can be dated.

q: Why can radiocarbon dating not be used on a bone thought to be about 200,000 years old?
c: After about 35 half-lives, far too little carbon-14 is left to measure.
The half-life of carbon-14 is longer than 200,000 years.
h: The method works to about 50,000 years. Why does it stop there?
w: About 35 half-lives: too little carbon-14 remains to measure.
x: Bone contains collagen, a protein full of carbon; younger bones are dated this way.
Carbon-14 keeps decaying; after 50,000 years so little is left that it cannot be measured reliably.
Carbon-14's half-life is 5730 years, far shorter than 200,000 years.

q: A geologist wants the age of a layer of volcanic rock thought to be about 2 million years old. Which isotope is the best choice?
h: The half-life should be long enough for the age being measured.
w: Volcanic rock, millions of years: potassium-40.
x: Carbon-14 dates only once-living material up to about 50,000 years; rock contains no carbon from a living thing.
Tritium dates water that fell as rain within the last several decades.
Iodine-131 would be gone within months; it is a medical isotope.

q: Complete this fission of uranium-235: <sup>1</sup><sub>0</sub>n + <sup>235</sup><sub>92</sub>U → <sup>144</sup><sub>56</sub>Ba + ? + 3 <sup>1</sup><sub>0</sub>n
h: Total the left side (do not forget the neutron), then count all 3 neutrons on the right.
w: A: 236 − 144 − 3 = 89. Z: 92 − 56 = 36: 8936Kr.
x: This counts the 3 neutrons as 1. The coefficient 3 adds 3 × 1 = 3 to the mass numbers.
This forgets the neutron on the left; fission starts when uranium-235 absorbs a neutron, so the left total is 236.
This gets Z wrong: 92 − 56 = 36, krypton, not 38.

q: What makes a fission chain reaction possible?
c: Each fission releases 2 or 3 neutrons, which can cause more fissions.
Each fission releases a gamma ray, which splits the next nucleus.
Each fission joins two light nuclei, which then split again.
The control rods give off neutrons that keep the reaction going.
h: What particle starts a fission, and how many come out?
w: Each fission releases more neutrons than it uses.
x: Gamma rays come out, but it is the neutrons that are absorbed and split uranium-235.
Joining light nuclei is fusion, the opposite process.
Control rods absorb neutrons to slow the chain reaction.

q: What is the critical mass of a fissionable material?
c: The smallest amount that can keep a chain reaction going
The mass of fuel used up by a reactor in one year
The mass lost and turned into energy in one fission
The largest amount that can be stored safely in one place
h: Think about neutrons escaping from a small piece.
w: Critical mass = the least fuel that keeps a chain reaction going.
x: This is not what critical mass describes; it is about whether a chain reaction can sustain itself.
The mass turned into energy (E = mc<sup>2</sup>) is tiny; critical mass is an amount of fuel.
The idea is the opposite: critical mass is the minimum amount for a self-sustaining chain reaction.

q: Which material are a reactor's control rods made of, and why?
c: Boron or cadmium, which absorb neutrons
Uranium oxide, which supplies the fuel
Water, which slows the neutrons down
h: The rods control the number of neutrons.
w: Control rods: boron or cadmium, neutron absorbers.
x: Uranium oxide pellets fill the fuel rods; control rods are not fuel.
Water is the moderator and coolant; it slows neutrons rather than absorbing them.
Lead shields gamma rays; control rods must absorb neutrons.

q: Per gram of fuel, how does the energy released by fusion compare with the energy released by fission?
c: Fusion releases even more energy than fission
Fusion releases less energy than fission
Fusion and fission release the same energy
Fusion absorbs energy instead of releasing it
h: What powers the Sun, and how much fuel does it use?
w: Fusion releases even more energy per gram.
x: This is backward; joining light nuclei releases more energy per gram than splitting heavy ones.
The amounts differ; fusion gives more per gram of fuel.
Fusion powers the Sun, so it releases a great deal of energy.

q: How does ionizing radiation most often damage DNA inside a cell?
c: It ionizes water, making free radicals such as ·OH that break bonds in DNA.
It makes the cell radioactive, so the cell decays.
It heats the cell until its DNA melts.
It changes the carbon atoms in DNA into nitrogen atoms.
h: What molecule is most common in a cell?
w: Ionized water makes free radicals that break DNA.
x: Gamma rays and X-rays deposit energy without changing nuclei, so the cell does not become radioactive.
Medical doses deposit far too little heat to matter; the damage is chemical, from ions and radicals.
Ionizing radiation removes electrons; it does not change nuclei in the cell.

q: Why can radiation be used to treat cancer?
c: Cancer cells divide rapidly, so their damaged DNA is copied before it can be repaired.
Radiation makes cancer cells radioactive, so they decay away.
Only cancer cells absorb radiation; healthy cells let it pass through.
Radiation heats a tumor until it melts.
h: Which cells are most sensitive to radiation?
w: Cancer cells divide rapidly, so radiation damage hits them hardest.
x: Gamma rays and X-rays change no nuclei, so the cells do not become radioactive.
Healthy cells are damaged too, which is why beams are aimed carefully from several directions.
The damage is chemical (ions and free radicals breaking DNA), not heat.

q: Radon-222 seeps from the soil into a home's basement. In which part of the body does it do most of its damage, and why?
c: The lungs: inhaled radon and its decay products emit alpha particles at lung cells.
The skin, because its alpha particles are all stopped there.
The bones, because the body takes up radon the way it takes up calcium.
Every organ equally, because radon gives off mostly gamma rays.
h: How does a gas get into the body?
w: The lungs: alpha particles are delivered right to lung cells.
x: The outer layer of skin is dead cells, which is why alpha particles from outside do little harm.
Radon is a noble gas that is breathed in and out, and it does not build into bone.
Radon-222 is an alpha emitter.

q: A patient who just received a tracer gives a dose rate of 48 μSv/h at 1.0 m. A technologist steps back to 4.0 m. What dose rate does she receive there?
h: Dose rate ∝ 1/distance<sup>2</sup>.
x: This divides by 4; the dose rate falls with the square of the distance.
This divides by 2 × 4 = 8; four times the distance divides the dose rate by 4<sup>2</sup> = 16.
This halves it; four times the distance cuts it to one-sixteenth.

q: A nuclear medicine technologist steps back from a patient, works faster, and draws up doses behind a lead-glass shield. What principle is she following?
c: ALARA: keep doses as low as reasonably achievable with time, distance, and shielding
Critical mass: keep the amount of tracer below the critical mass
Half-life: wait 10 half-lives before going near any patient
Inverse ionization: stand closer so the radiation spreads out
h: Three tools: time, distance, shielding.
w: ALARA, using time, distance, and shielding.
x: Critical mass is about chain reactions in fission fuel, not tracers.
Waiting 10 half-lives is used for stored waste; patient care cannot wait days.
Standing closer raises the dose rate; distance lowers it.

q: Why are boxed, sealed surgical gloves sterilized with gamma rays rather than beta particles?
c: Gamma rays can pass through the sealed boxes, and beta particles cannot.
Beta particles would leave the gloves radioactive after treatment.
Gamma rays are more strongly ionizing than beta particles are.
Beta particles cannot damage the DNA of bacteria on the gloves.
h: Which property matters for a sealed, boxed product?
w: The gloves are sterilized after they are sealed in boxes, so the radiation must get through the packaging. Gamma rays penetrate the sealed boxes, while beta particles are stopped within a few millimeters of material. Gamma rays are actually less ionizing than beta particles, so ionizing power is not why they are chosen.
x: Neither beta particles nor gamma rays change the nuclei in the gloves.
Gamma rays are the least ionizing of the common kinds of radiation, so ionizing power is not the reason.
Beta particles are ionizing too, so they can damage bacterial DNA if they reach it.

q: How do X-rays differ from gamma rays?
c: X-rays are made outside the nucleus in a tube; gamma rays come from nuclei.
X-rays come from decaying nuclei; gamma rays come from machines.
X-rays are particles with mass; gamma rays are a form of light.
X-rays are too weak to ionize atoms; gamma rays are ionizing.
h: Where does each kind of radiation come from?
w: X-rays from a tube (outside the nucleus); gamma rays from decaying nuclei.
x: This swaps the sources of the two kinds of radiation.
Both X-rays and gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation, with no mass.
Both are ionizing, which is why X-ray exposures are justified and kept small (ALARA).

q: For most people in the United States, which source gives the largest share of natural background radiation?
c: Radon gas from uranium in rocks and soil
Emissions from nearby nuclear power plants
Cosmic rays from space reaching the ground
Potassium-40 in the food we eat
h: Which natural source is a gas that collects indoors?
w: Radon is the largest natural source of background radiation.
x: Nuclear power plants add only a tiny amount to the dose of people living nearby.
Cosmic rays add to background radiation, more at high altitude and on flights, but they are not the largest natural source.
Potassium-40 in food and in the body contributes, but less than radon.

q: Which tissue is most sensitive to radiation damage?
c: Bone marrow, which makes blood cells
Adult nerve cells in the brain
Adult muscle in the arms and legs
h: Which cells are most sensitive: rapidly dividing ones or slowly dividing ones?
w: Bone marrow: its rapidly dividing cells are the most sensitive.
x: Adult nerve cells rarely divide, so they are among the least sensitive.
Adult muscle cells divide slowly, so they are less sensitive.
Enamel is mostly mineral with no living, dividing cells.
